problem_domains.description: The paper focuses on computing the fair value of derivative contracts such as options, including European, American, and basket options.
problem_domains.quote: In this article, the set of algorithms to be explored corresponds to the pricing of financial derivatives and Value-at-Risk (VaR) computation.

problem_domains.description: The paper addresses the problem of forecasting portfolio losses via VaR as a key risk measure.
problem_domains.quote: In the second case, the VaR is a risk measure so that the objective is to forecast the losses of future operations.

problem_domains.description: The paper considers risk management of derivatives, including portfolio risk metrics such as VaR and CVaR.
problem_domains.quote: In the second part of Sect. 2, financial risk management concepts are covered such as Market Risk and Credit Portfolio Management, as well as key risk portfolio metrics such as Value-at-Risk and Conditional Value-at-Risk (or Expected Shortfall).

problem_domains.description: The paper details the problem of computing fair values for European vanilla call and put options under stochastic models.
problem_domains.quote: For vanilla options, the payoffs only depend on the value of the underlying at expiry date T.
problem_domains.location: Page 4, Section 2.1.1 Financial Derivatives and Options

problem_domains.description: The paper treats the valuation of American options, which include early exercise features and lead to optimal stopping problems.
problem_domains.quote: In the case of American options, the early exercise opportunity implies the replacement of the PDE problem (10) by a linear complementarity problem associated to the Black-Scholes differential operator:

problem_domains.description: The paper discusses options whose payoff depends on multiple underlying assets, increasing dimensionality.
problem_domains.quote: Options that depend on a set of assets are also traded in the financial markets and are known as basket options.

problem_domains.description: The paper highlights computational challenges when pricing derivatives with many underlying assets or factors.
problem_domains.quote: the “curse of dimensionality”, that arises when the number of underlying assets or stochastic factors becomes large.

problem_domains.problem: portfolio credit risk and loss distribution estimation
problem_domains.description: The paper addresses modeling and simulating portfolio credit losses for many counterparties to compute risk measures.
problem_domains.quote: As the credit quality of the counterparty (captured by the asset value in the Merton model) is correlated, this problem is closely related to the basket option covered earlier, but with the additional complexity of having different barriers.

problem_domains.problem: dimensionality reduction in credit portfolio models
problem_domains.description: The paper discusses the need to reduce dimensionality in large credit portfolios using factor models and PCA.
problem_domains.quote: Given its complexity and high dimensionality, credit portfolio modelling relies on dimensionality reduction techniques such as factor models and Principal Component Analysis (PCA).

problem_domains.problem: estimation of VaR and CVaR from loss distributions
problem_domains.description: The paper defines and focuses on computing VaR and CVaR as tail-based risk measures from portfolio loss distributions.
problem_domains.quote: We consider two well-known measures of risk, the Value-at-Risk (VaR) and the Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) (also known as Expected Shortfall).
problem_domains.location: Page 8, Section 2.2 Risk Measures for Derivatives Portfolios

problem_domains.problem: slow convergence of classical Monte Carlo for pricing and risk
problem_domains.description: The paper notes that classical Monte Carlo has O(1/√M) convergence, which is slow for many applications.
problem_domains.quote: Therefore, the quadratic error of the Monte Carlo estimate tends to zero with order O(1∕√M) when M tends to infinity, which is considered slow for many applications.

problem_domains.description: Estimation of Value at Risk and Conditional Value at Risk from loss distributions, especially in high-confidence tail regimes where Monte Carlo is inefficient.
problem_domains.quote: The VaR (and the CVaR) are intended to prevent extreme events of big losses, so the quantile /u1D6FC is usually between 95% and 99.9% depending on the application. In such regimes, Monte Carlo is rather inefficient, specially for the CVaR computation, since the number of samples in the area of interest is usually not sufficient to provide an acceptable precision.
problem_domains.location: Page 11, paragraph starting 'The VaR (and the CVaR) are intended...'

problem_domains.problem: High-dimensional Monte Carlo for pricing and risk
problem_domains.description: Computation of expectation values for pricing and risk problems over high-dimensional domains where classical Monte Carlo becomes costly.
problem_domains.quote: As we saw in Sects. 2.1.3 and 2.2.3, the computation of expectation values constitutes the basis for many pricing and risk problems. Such a computation is normally performed by means of classical Monte Carlo methods. The exponential growth of the dimension of the Hilbert space with the number of qubits, however, suggests that an alternative quantum implementation for Monte Carlo could be in a better position than its classical counterparts, especially over domains with a high dimensionality.
problem_domains.location: Page 12, first full paragraph under 3.1 Quantum‑Accelerated Monte Carlo

problem_domains.problem: Option pricing as expectation of payoff
problem_domains.description: Pricing of (including path-dependent) options formulated as computing the expected value of a payoff function under a risk-neutral probability distribution.
problem_domains.quote: As presented in Eq. (8 ), the option pricing problem can be formulated as the computation of the expected value of a payoff function with respect to a probability distribution:10
problem_domains.location: Page 14, start of 3.1.3 Applications to Option Pricing

problem_domains.description: Risk analysis requiring precise estimation of the tail of loss distributions for portfolios of derivatives, which is demanding for Monte Carlo.
problem_domains.quote: Nevertheless, risk analysis problems require a precise estimation of the tail of a distribution, which constitute a more demanding task in terms of Monte Carlo samplings. On top of that, the problem usually is highly dimensional, because portfolios of various derivatives are usually considered.
problem_domains.location: Page 15, first full paragraph under 3.1.4 Applications to Risk Analysis

problem_domains.problem: Computing probability of large losses and corresponding VaR level
problem_domains.description: Estimating the probability of losses exceeding a threshold and determining the maximal loss corresponding to a given confidence level.
problem_domains.quote: In risk assessment, one can be interested in estimating the probability of experiencing a future loss exceeding a predetermined value, according to, for example, the definition of the VaR and the CVaR risk measures as in Sect. 2.2. Such a question can again be addressed by means of a comparator. More often, one is interested in fixing a (high) confidence level /u1D6FC and asking which maximal loss corresponds to it.
problem_domains.location: Page 15, paragraph starting 'In risk assessment, one can be interested...'

problem_domains.problem: Solving Black–Scholes and related financial PDEs
problem_domains.description: Numerical solution of Black–Scholes-type partial differential equations for derivative pricing, including mapping them to forms amenable to quantum simulation.
problem_domains.quote: Following [36], the quantum approaches rely on the observation that the financial PDEs can be mapped into the propagation governed by an appropriate Hamiltonian operator.
problem_domains.location: Page 16, first paragraph under 3.2 Quantum PDEs

problem_domains.problem: Principal Component Analysis for risk and pricing models
problem_domains.description: Dimensionality reduction of covariance structures in pricing and risk models via PCA.
problem_domains.quote: Principal Component Analysis is a classical mathematical technique that is widely used in quantitative finance for dimensionality reduction; not only for both pricing problems (as Sect.  2.1.1) and in risk models (as the ones in Sect.  2.2.2), but also for stock value forecasting (usually in combination with other machine learning techniques).
problem_domains.location: Page 11, paragraph starting 'Principal Component Analysis is a classical...'

problem_domains.problem: Eigen-decomposition of covariance matrices for PCA
problem_domains.description: Computing eigenvalues and eigenvectors of large, dense covariance matrices used in financial PCA.
problem_domains.quote: The first step behind PCA is to calculate the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix Σ∈ℝ N × ℝN , which is Hermitian and positive semi-definite.
problem_domains.location: Page 18, first paragraph under 3.3.1 Quantum Principal Component Analysis

problem_domains.problem: Regression-based pricing, especially for early-exercise options
problem_domains.description: Using regression and linear system solving in Monte Carlo pricing of options with early exercise such as American options.
problem_domains.quote: Classical and more advanced (neural networks-based) regression methodologies are greatly appreciated in derivative pricing problems, in particular for options with early exercise, like American options (see Sect.  2.1.1), when they are priced by Monte Carlo methods.

problem_domains.problem: Deep learning for PDEs, BSDEs, and other finance tasks
problem_domains.description: Application of deep neural networks to solve PDEs, BSDEs, inverse option pricing, and counterparty credit risk.
problem_domains.quote: As it is the case for many other disciplines, computational finance greatly benefits from this new computational paradigm, with successful developments on numerical solutions for PDEs or Backward Stochastic Differential Equations (BSDE), inverse option pricing problems, counterparty credit risk computations, etc.
problem_domains.location: Page 19, paragraph under 3.3.3 Quantum Neural Networks and Deep Learning

problem_domains.problem: Loading probability distributions for pricing and VaR
problem_domains.description: Efficiently constructing a quantum circuit that loads a given probability distribution over scenarios or paths, which is required for QAMC in pricing and VaR.
problem_domains.quote: The main implicit assumption in QAMC is the existence of an efficient oracle which loads the probability distribution. Both for pricing and VaR, loading the distribution means that it is necessary to create a circuit for a unitary operation P such that:

problem_domains.problem: Simulation of SDEs for pricing distributions
problem_domains.description: Generating the underlying probability distribution for pricing via simulation of stochastic differential equations, which dominates classical computational cost.
problem_domains.quote: In pricing, the distribution to be loaded has to be previously generated through the simulation of a SDE. As it was discussed in the first part of this survey, the simulation of the SDE consumes most of the computing resources.
problem_domains.location: Page 20, paragraph starting 'In pricing, the distribution to be loaded...'

problem_domains.description: The survey discusses how loading probability distributions into quantum states directly benefits Value-at-Risk calculations, which require empirical distributions.
problem_domains.quote: 1. Loading a probability distribution: the direct benefits in this matter goes to VaR problems.

problem_domains.description: VaR calculations always require loading an empirical probability distribution into the quantum register, making state loading a key bottleneck.
problem_domains.quote: As opposed to pricing where there are cases in which the probability distribution can be generated sinthetically, in VaR we always need to load an empirical distribution. Thus, the loading step is of particular importance for VaR.

problem_domains.description: The survey treats pricing problems where payoff functions must be loaded and probability distributions may be generated synthetically or via stochastic simulation.
problem_domains.quote: 3. Loading a payoff function: this case is only relevant for pricing.

problem_domains.problem: Simulation of stochastic differential equations for underlying assets
problem_domains.description: The document frames the need to simulate discrete stochastic processes that approximate SDEs for underlying assets, especially when no analytical solution exists or options are path dependent.
problem_domains.quote: With “generative approach” we refer to the actual simulation of the discrete stochastic processes which generate the desired approximate distribution. The discrete stochastic approach is particularly important when the underlying asset SDE does not admit an analytical formulation, or when the option is path dependent (thus requiring the knowledge of the distribution of the underlying at intermediate times before maturity) as it usually happens in pricing.

problem_domains.description: The survey highlights the challenge of loading payoff functions, especially arbitrary or non-piecewise-linear payoffs, into quantum circuits for expectation value computation.
problem_domains.quote: The task of computing the expectation value of a payoff  function with respect to a probability distribution, see Eq. (53), requires that both be loaded into the quantum circuit, accordingly to the pipeline depicted in Fig. 2.

problem_domains.problem: Implementation of payoff functions for European vanilla options and piecewise linear payoffs
problem_domains.description: The paper notes that European vanilla option payoffs are relatively easy to implement via comparator circuits, but general piecewise linear payoffs already increase circuit complexity.
problem_domains.quote: The payoff functions for European vanilla options, see Eq. (1), are relatively easy to implement by means of a comparator circuit. As long as the payoff function is piecewise linear, one can generalize the approach implemented for the European vanilla contracts. Nonetheless, this would already entail an increased level of complexity in the quantum circuit; for instance, any separation point between two linear regions would require a comparator circuit19.

problem_domains.description: For arbitrary payoff functions, loading them into a quantum state that already encodes the probability distribution can be more complex than loading the distribution itself.
problem_domains.quote: In a completely general case, i.e. for arbitrary payoff, its loading problem can be even more complicated than that of the probability distribution function.

problem_domains.problem: Derivatives pricing and financial risk management (general)
problem_domains.description: The survey addresses the broader financial problems of derivative pricing and financial risk management, including VaR and PDE-based approaches.
problem_domains.quote: While this progress is very encouraging, further work will be required to prove that Quantum Computing can deliver real-world advantage to the areas of derivative pricing and financial risk management.

problem_domains.problem: Solution of PDEs arising in finance
problem_domains.description: The document discusses solving partial differential equations on quantum computers with applications to derivative pricing and risk management.
problem_domains.quote: An area that is also showing some interesting results is the solution of PDEs using quantum computers with applications to derivative pricing and risk management.

solution_approaches.approach: quantum alternatives to classical Monte Carlo based on Quantum Amplitude Estimation
solution_approaches.description: The paper reviews quantum Monte Carlo-style methods for pricing and VaR that rely on Quantum Amplitude Estimation and its variants.
solution_approaches.quote: Section 3 starts discussing quantum alternatives to classical Monte Carlo. The cornerstone of the quantum alternatives to Monte Carlo rely on Quantum Amplitude Estimation and more modern variations on this technique.

solution_approaches.approach: quantum methods for solving derivative pricing models using PDEs
solution_approaches.description: The paper considers quantum algorithms that tackle PDE-based formulations of derivative pricing problems.
solution_approaches.quote: Later on, still in Sect. 3, quantum methods for solving derivative pricing models using PDEs are also discussed.

solution_approaches.approach: numerical quantum techniques closer to Machine Learning for pricing and VaR
solution_approaches.description: The paper introduces quantum numerical techniques for pricing and VaR that are conceptually related to machine learning approaches.
solution_approaches.quote: In the third block of Sect. 3 we introduce some numerical quantum techniques for pricing and VaR which, at least in spirit, are closer to Machine Learning.

solution_approaches.approach: efficient loading or generation of probability distributions in a quantum computer
solution_approaches.description: The paper identifies efficient quantum state preparation of probability distributions as a key technical component for quantum Monte Carlo-style algorithms.
solution_approaches.quote: Section 3 concludes with a review of the key remaining challenges for quantum alternatives to Monte Carlo to deliver their potential advantage, namely, the efficient loading or generation of probability distributions in a quantum computer and the computation of the payoff functions in pricing problems.

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum-Accelerated Monte Carlo (QAMC)
solution_approaches.description: Quantum algorithms that implement Monte Carlo-style expectation estimation using amplitude amplification and estimation to achieve quadratic precision scaling.
solution_approaches.quote: Quantum-Accelerated Monte Carlo8 for the computation of the expected value of a function is usually divided in four steps (see Fig.  2):

solution_approaches.approach: Amplitude amplification
solution_approaches.description: Use of Grover-style operators to increase the probability of measuring 'good' states corresponding to desired outcomes.
solution_approaches.quote: the amplitude amplification algorithm gives us a strategy to enhance the probability of measuring � ̃Ψ1⟩ , namely the “good” or marked state.

solution_approaches.approach: Original amplitude estimation with inverse Quantum Fourier Transform
solution_approaches.description: Amplitude estimation using controlled Grover iterations and an inverse Quantum Fourier Transform on an auxiliary register.
solution_approaches.quote: The path suggested in the original paper [15] is to adopt an inverse quantum Fourier transform, see Fig.  3.
solution_approaches.location: Page 13, first paragraph under 'Original Amplitude Estimation'

solution_approaches.approach: Amplitude estimation with Max Likelihood
solution_approaches.description: Amplitude estimation avoiding QFT by collecting measurement data for different Grover powers and using classical maximum likelihood post-processing.
solution_approaches.quote: One interesting possibility to avoid the inverse Quantum Fourier transform has been suggested in [84] and it relies on classical post-processing.
solution_approaches.location: Page 13, paragraph under 'Quantum Amplitude Amplification and Estimation with Max Likelihood'

solution_approaches.approach: Iterative Quantum Amplitude Estimation
solution_approaches.description: A variant of amplitude estimation without quantum phase estimation, reducing qubits and gates while maintaining quadratic speed-up.
solution_approaches.quote: In [39] a different variant of quantum amplitude estimation is considered, which does not need quantum phase estimation, that is, it avoids the estimation of /u1D703 through an inverse Quantum Fourier Transform.
solution_approaches.location: Page 13–14, first paragraph under 'Iterative Quantum Amplitude Estimation'

solution_approaches.approach: Power-law amplitude estimation
solution_approaches.description: An amplitude estimation algorithm that optimizes the sampling schedule using a power-law trade-off between total oracle calls and depth.
solution_approaches.quote: The Power-law algorithm (sometimes referred to as Kerenidis-Prakash algorithm) refines the Max Likelihood algorithm of [84].

solution_approaches.approach: QoPrime amplitude estimation
solution_approaches.description: Amplitude estimation based on the Chinese Remainder Theorem, using coprime sampling schedules to combine low-accuracy samples into high-accuracy estimates.
solution_approaches.quote: The QoPrime algorithm follows the same trade-off between N and D as the Power-law algorithm, however its strategy is based on a result from number theory, that is known as Chinese Remainder Theorem.

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum coins
solution_approaches.description: Grover-family algorithms that load the integrand function directly into amplitudes (direct embedding) instead of its square root, avoiding inverse QFT.
solution_approaches.quote: Although belonging to the same family of Grover algorithms, the quantum coin loads the integrand function (and not its square root) into the quantum state amplitude.

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum comparator circuits and binary search for VaR/CVaR
solution_approaches.description: Use of quantum comparator circuits to implement payoff activation or loss thresholds, combined with binary search to find VaR levels.
solution_approaches.quote: Such a question can again be addressed by means of a comparator. More often, one is interested in fixing a (high) confidence level /u1D6FC and asking which maximal loss corresponds to it. This question can be addressed combining a comparator with a binary search algorithm [26, 27].
solution_approaches.location: Page 15, paragraph starting 'In risk assessment, one can be interested...'

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum multi-level Monte Carlo
solution_approaches.description: Quantum generalization of multi-level Monte Carlo where a quantum circuit solves each Monte Carlo sub-problem in a telescopic sum.
solution_approaches.quote: As a final remark on quantum-enhanced Monte Carlo techniques, we refer to [7 ] for the quantum generalization of the classical multi-level Monte Carlo strategy [32].
solution_approaches.location: Page 15, last paragraph under 3.1.4 Applications to Risk Analysis

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum PDEs via Hamiltonian propagation with ĤBS
solution_approaches.description: Mapping Black–Scholes PDE to a Schrödinger-like equation with a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian ĤBS and simulating its propagation using QFT and Cartan decomposition.
solution_approaches.quote: In [36] they consider the Hamiltonian (68) and exploit the fact that it is diagonal in momentum space. Thus, by means of a quantum Fourier transform, and its inverse, they are able to work with a diagonal propagator, which admits an efficient decomposition in the Cartan basis.
solution_approaches.location: Page 17, first paragraph under 3.2.1 Propagating with ̂HBS

solution_approaches.approach: Imaginary-time propagation with ĤHE
solution_approaches.description: Transforming Black–Scholes to a heat equation and then to an imaginary-time Schrödinger equation, solved via variational imaginary-time evolution.
solution_approaches.quote: A quantum algorithm for imaginary-time propagation has been developed in the field of quantum chemistry [63]. 13 It assumes to deal with a Hamiltonian
solution_approaches.location: Page 17, first paragraph under 3.2.2 Imaginary‑Time Propagation with ̂HHE

solution_approaches.approach: Variational imaginary-time evolution (McLachlan principle)
solution_approaches.description: Using a parametrized circuit and McLachlan’s variational principle to evolve parameters according to a linear system and approximate ground states relevant to pricing PDEs.
solution_approaches.quote: More technically, the imaginary-time method entails considering a McLachlan variational principle

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum Principal Component Analysis (QPCA)
solution_approaches.description: Using quantum algorithms to obtain eigenvalues/eigenvectors of covariance matrices treated as density matrices, potentially with exponential speedup.
solution_approaches.quote: Another possibility is to work with the covariance matrix Σ as a density matrix (usually represented as /u1D70C ), and make a Quantum Principal Component Analysis (QPCA).
solution_approaches.location: Page 18, paragraph starting 'Another possibility is to work with the covariance matrix...'

solution_approaches.approach: Variational QPCA via density matrix expansion
solution_approaches.description: Expressing the covariance matrix as a sum over an operator basis and learning a unitary that diagonalizes it using variational hybrid algorithms.
solution_approaches.quote: Recently, [92] suggested to calculate the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of Σ through a variational algorithm, by using the density matrix expansion

solution_approaches.approach: HHL-based quantum regression
solution_approaches.description: Using the HHL algorithm for solving linear systems as a subroutine in quantum regression methods for pricing.
solution_approaches.quote: The HHL algorithm proposed in [43] is a first relevant representative algorithm for solving linear systems, allowing to diagonalize some special matrices with exponential speedup. Then, the HHL algorithm was employed to perform a regression on a quantum computer in [90].

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum kernel estimation and Gaussian process QML
solution_approaches.description: Quantum machine learning approaches such as quantum kernel estimation and Gaussian process models for regression-like tasks.
solution_approaches.quote: Other quantum-based techniques like Quantum Kernel Estimation  [28] and QML with Gaussian processes [94] have been recently proposed.

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum neural networks (QNNs) and deep learning
solution_approaches.description: Fully quantum neural network architectures and training methods, including for function or distribution loading.
solution_approaches.quote: Another research line consists in the algorithms based on a fully Quantum Neural Network (QNN). In the last few years, many works on QNN advanced training have been proposed, among which we highlight [ 10, 23]. One of the main applications of QNNs is the function (or distribution) loading.
solution_approaches.location: Page 19–20, paragraph under 3.3.3 Quantum Neural Networks and Deep Learning

solution_approaches.approach: Grover approach for loading probability distributions
solution_approaches.description: A Grover-based method discretizes a continuous probability density into regions and iteratively maps conditioned probabilities into amplitudes of a quantum state.
solution_approaches.quote: Grover Approach [40] proposed a general methodology to load integrable probability distributions into the states efficiently.

solution_approaches.approach: Variational Quantum Circuits for approximated state loading
solution_approaches.description: Parametric quantum circuits are trained to approximate the amplitudes of a target probability distribution, potentially via QGANs.
solution_approaches.quote: • Variational Quantum Circuits: create an ad-hoc circuit which approximates the amplitudes [68].

solution_approaches.approach: Tensor Networks techniques for state preparation
solution_approaches.description: Tensor network ansatzes, particularly matrix product states, are used to encode amplitude functions efficiently into quantum circuits.
solution_approaches.quote: • Tensor Networks techniques [31, 48, 72].

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum Generative Adversarial Networks (QGANs)
solution_approaches.description: QGANs use a parametric quantum generator circuit trained adversarially to transform an initial distribution into a desired probability distribution for option pricing and other tasks.

problem_solution_mappings.quote: This generic idea of loading an approximated version of the state, aiming to have an efficient process, can take different practical paths. key_claims.claim: Quantum computing promises faster responses for computationally demanding financial algorithms and can address problems that are currently intractable.
key_claims.quote: For an increasing number of cases, quantum computing promises faster responses that can provide solutions to up-to-now intractable problems.

key_claims.claim: There is no known analytical solution for the American option linear complementarity problem, so numerical methods are required.
key_claims.quote: There is no known analytical solution to this problem and therfore it needs to be solved numerically.
key_claims.location: Page 7, American options PDE complementarity problem

key_claims.claim: Classical Monte Carlo is inefficient for VaR and especially CVaR in high-confidence tail regimes.
key_claims.quote: In such regimes, Monte Carlo is rather inefficient, specially for the CVaR computation, since the number of samples in the area of interest is usually not sufficient to provide an acceptable precision.
key_claims.location: Page 11, paragraph on VaR/CVaR and Monte Carlo

key_claims.claim: QAMC algorithms offer a theoretical quadratic speed-up in precision over classical Monte Carlo.
key_claims.quote:
They entail a theoretical quadratic speed-up with respect to classical Monte Carlo. More precisely, if the precision for classical Monte Carlo sampling generically scales as M− 1
2 , where M is the number of samples, quantum algorithms have a theoretical precision scaling as M−1.
key_claims.location: Page 12, bullet list of QAMC properties

key_claims.claim: The inverse Quantum Fourier Transform is a serious bottleneck for original amplitude estimation on near-term devices.
key_claims.quote: The inverse Quantum Fourier transform adopted by the original amplitude estimation algorithm [15] is resource demanding and thus constitutes a serious bottleneck, especially in relation to current or near-future technologies.

key_claims.claim: Iterative quantum amplitude estimation reduces qubit and gate requirements while maintaining quadratic speed-up.
key_claims.quote: As such, the suggested implementation is able to reduce the number of qubits and gates, making the overall algorithm lighter. The analysis in [39] focuses on a rigorous study of the quadratic quantum speed-up for their algorithm.
key_claims.location: Page 13–14, paragraph under 'Iterative Quantum Amplitude Estimation'

key_claims.claim: Power-law and QoPrime algorithms interpolate between quantum and classical Monte Carlo by trading off total oracle calls and depth.
key_claims.quote:
Roughly, Power-law and QoPrime algorithms interpolate between the quantum and classical cases playing with the trade-off between N  and D , at fixed

key_claims.claim: Quantum PDE approaches based on ĤBS may offer exponential speedup in the propagation subroutine but face open problems in loading models and payoffs.
key_claims.quote: They study the possibility of truncating the Hamiltonian retaining just a polynomial number of interactions and, on this basis, they claim an exponential speedup in the Hamiltonian propagation subroutine. Nevertheless, an overall exponential speedup for the entire pipeline would require efficient loading of the uncertainty model and of the payoff function. These issues remain as open problems.

key_claims.claim: The transformation to a pure heat equation used for imaginary-time propagation is specific to Black–Scholes and may not generalize.
key_claims.quote: First, the transformation to a pure heat equation, ( 71), occurs for the Black-Scholes model but is expected not to hold when generalizing it.
key_claims.location: Page 18, paragraph starting 'Also this approach presents some drawbacks.'

key_claims.claim: Most QML algorithms assume QRAM, which is not expected to be realizable in the near future.
key_claims.quote: Note however that most quantum machine learning algorithms working with classical data assume the availability of a Quantum Random Access Memory (QRAM), which are not expected to be physically realizable in the near future [14].
key_claims.location: Page 18, paragraph under 3.3 Quantum Machine Learning

key_claims.claim: QPCA has theoretical exponential speed but practical scalability is limited to O(N²) operations.
key_claims.quote: In general, these facts limit the scalability of QPCA to O(N2) operations. However, it could still exhibit better performance than the general classical complexity, which corresponding to O(N3) operations.
key_claims.location: Page 18, last paragraph of 3.3.1 Quantum Principal Component Analysis

key_claims.claim: The main implicit assumption in QAMC is an efficient probability-loading oracle, which is critical and often unrealistic.
key_claims.quote: The main implicit assumption in QAMC is the existence of an efficient oracle which loads the probability distribution.

key_claims.claim: When accounting for SDE simulation and distribution loading, there is no rigorous evidence of quadratic speed-up for QAMC in pricing.
key_claims.quote: Indeed, the claims of a quadratic speed-up of the QAMC over the CMC for financial applications—in general—do not take into account the generation step. If we compare both QAMC and CMC under the same conditions, with the approaches proposed in the literature, we will find that there is no rigorous evidence for the quadratic speed-up.
key_claims.location: Page 20, paragraph starting 'In pricing, the distribution to be loaded...'

key_claims.claim: A quadratic speed-up is not sufficient for practical quantum advantage due to large constant overheads such as error correction.
key_claims.quote: an important (negative) claim has been described in [8], where it is argued that a quadratic speed-up is not sufficient to obtain a quantum advantage, mainly due to the—constant but large—resource overheads (needed for error correction).
key_claims.location: Page 20, paragraph starting 'Many ideal algorithms studied in the literature...'

key_claims.claim: Path-dependent derivatives may be necessary to reach regimes where quantum technologies can provide advantage, but current resource estimates are prohibitive.
key_claims.quote: They argue that the complexity of the pricing task implied by path dependence is a necessary ingredient to find a regime where quantum technologies can lead to an advantage with respect to their classical counterparts. However, the benchmark cases are showed to need 7.5k  logical qubits and a depth of 46 million T-gates and a clock-rate of 10 MHz (current quantum technologies moves on the order of 10 kHz). These are recognized as markedly prohibitive for the moment, yet they set an order-of-magnitude scenario, useful to frame further research and strategy.

key_claims.claim: Loading the probability distribution is often the main bottleneck in quantum amplitude Monte Carlo for finance.
key_claims.quote: Loading the necessary state into a quantum register in order to initialize an algorithm constitutes often the main bottleneck. For example, [31, 67] show that in QAMC the overall calculation time is dominated by the (asymptotic) time to load the probability distribution as

key_claims.claim: General methods to load exact probability distributions have poor scalability with the number of points.
key_claims.quote: The main problem of the first two methods is the poor scalability with the number of points that we need to load.

key_claims.claim: Approximating the quantum state to be loaded can reduce resource requirements at the cost of accuracy.
key_claims.quote: In order to seek for efficient loading algorithms, we can give up techniques which load the exact function in the quantum state and explore the possibility of approximating the state to be loaded. In this way we lower the resources necessary to load the state at the cost of accuracy and exploit the fact that we are working with a specific subset of functions.

key_claims.claim: Grover-based state preparation methods may not yield a speedup for Monte Carlo according to recent works.
key_claims.quote: However, some recent works dispute the possibility of a speed-up when this method is used for Monte Carlo [19, 45, 52].

key_claims.claim: Variational methods lack clear guarantees on loading performance and speed-up due to optimization uncertainty.
key_claims.quote: In general, variational methods do not provide a clear path to get the sought for speed-up. Specifically, it is difficult to guarantee the loading performance by means of rigorous bounds. This is mainly due to the uncertainty associated to the optimization of the parameters [19].

key_claims.claim: Tensor network techniques offer promising, efficient, and scalable encoding of amplitude functions but extension to general empirical distributions is not yet known.
key_claims.quote: Matrix product states (MPS) constitute a widely used class of tensor network ansatzes. These have been long studied in the context of quantum computation [76] and have been recently claimed to allow for an efficient and scalable encoding of explicit amplitude functions with a high fidelity, relying just on linear-depth quantum circuits [48]. ... Although being a promising method, the extension to a general empirical data-based probability is not, to our knowledge, yet known and needs further research.

key_claims.claim: Loading arbitrary payoff functions can be more complicated than loading probability distributions and scales inefficiently if done pointwise.
key_claims.quote: In a completely general case, i.e. for arbitrary payoff, its loading problem can be even more complicated than that of the probability distribution function. ... For small size examples, the payoff can be loaded pointwise. However this is clearly an approach which scales inefficiently and cannot be planned for real applications.

key_claims.claim: Further work is required to demonstrate real-world quantum advantage in derivative pricing and financial risk management, especially on NISQ devices.
key_claims.quote: While this progress is very encouraging, further work will be required to prove that Quantum Computing can deliver real-world advantage to the areas of derivative pricing and financial risk management. Especially if this advantage is to be delivered on Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum technology with limitations to both the number of logical qubits and the width of quantum circuits.

key_claims.claim: Efficient methods for loading probability distributions and representing payoff functions as unitaries are still needed.
key_claims.quote: Further theoretical work is needed in order to find efficient (ideally optimal) ways to load probability distributions to quantum registers, as well as efficient mathematical representations of payoff functions using unitary transforms that can be easily implemented in a quantum circuit.

key_claims.claim: Quantum algorithms for PDEs in finance have not yet demonstrated an advantage over classical methods.
key_claims.quote: While exciting, these approaches have not yet been able to prove whether quantum algorithms can provide an advantage over their classical counterparts.

key_claims.claim: QML can be robust on noisy hardware and projected quantum kernels may offer quantum advantage in learning, but real-world problems remain too high-dimensional for classical handling.
key_claims.quote: Lastly, relatively recent advances in both classical and Quantum Machine Learning algorithms for solving PDEs are also exciting, especially because it has been shown that QML can be robust when implemented in noisy hardware. Furthermore, QML algorithms can present some interesting theoretical advantages over their classical counterparts, see for example [49], where the authors introduce the concept of “projected quantum kernel” to show numerical results that promise a quantum advantage in learning algorithms. These kernels work by projecting the quantum states to an approximate classical representation, helping to reduce the dimensionality of the problem, however for real-world examples the dimension would be still too large to be handled efficiently using a classical computer.

key_claims.claim: Research into financial applications of quantum computing is accelerating, but important breakthroughs across the technology stack are still needed.
key_claims.quote: In summary, research into financial applications of quantum computing is accelerating with new ideas emerging at rapid pace and while important breakthroughs across the technology stack will be needed to make the approach viable, the recent accelerated publication of important results is encouraging.

maturity_indicators.quote: We then describe some of the most popular quantum algorithms for pricing and VaR. Finally, we discuss the main remaining challenges for the quantum algorithms to achieve their potential advantages.
Nevertheless, an overall exponential speedup for the entire pipeline would require efficient loading of the uncertainty model and of the payoff function. These issues remain as open problems.

Many ideal algorithms studied in the literature are not viable on current or near-future quantum technology 14. They usually require either an exceedingly large number of qubits or involve too deep a circuit with respect to the realistic coherence time, or both.
maturity_indicators.location: Page 20, paragraph starting 'Many ideal algorithms studied in the literature...'

maturity_indicators.quote: However, the benchmark cases are showed to need 7.5k  logical qubits and a depth of 46 million T-gates and a clock-rate of 10 MHz (current quantum technologies moves on the order of 10 kHz). These are recognized as markedly prohibitive for the moment, yet they set an order-of-magnitude scenario, useful to frame further research and strategy.
Especially if this advantage is to be delivered on Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum technology with limitations to both the number of logical qubits and the width of quantum circuits.

Lastly, relatively recent advances in both classical and Quantum Machine Learning algorithms for solving PDEs are also exciting, especially because it has been shown that QML can be robust when implemented in noisy hardware.

open_questions.question: Can the imaginary-time propagation approach be generalized beyond Black–Scholes, and how efficient is the classical solution of the parameter evolution system?
open_questions.quote: First, the transformation to a pure heat equation, ( 71), occurs for the Black-Scholes model but is expected not to hold when generalizing it. Secondly, the evolution of the parameters is governed by (76) which is solved with classical computing techniques. Its efficiency and scaling properties have not been assessed thoroughly.
open_questions.location: Page 18, paragraph starting 'Also this approach presents some drawbacks.'

open_questions.question: Is the variational QPCA procedure efficient in the general case for large financial covariance matrices?
open_questions.quote: Once U(Θ) is found (or—at least—suitably approximated), the eigenvalues can be computed directly by measuring probabilities on the computational basis. It is nevertheless not clear yet whether this procedure is efficient in the general case.

open_questions.question: How can full quantum algorithms for pricing and VaR be designed so that subroutine speed-ups translate into end-to-end quantum advantage?
open_questions.quote: These problems provide concrete examples about possible issues encountered in designing full quantum algorithms able to reach a quantum advantage. Almost any speed-up concentrated in a subroutine of an overarching inefficient algorithm, however interesting, is clearly not sufficient to reach quantum advantage.
open_questions.location: Page 20, paragraph starting 'These problems provide concrete examples...'

open_questions.question: What are realistic thresholds for quantum advantage in finance when considering not only time complexity but also energy consumption and cost?
open_questions.quote: We are here implicitly referring (as it often happens) to quantum advantage in terms of scaling of the execution time. This is only a part of a bigger picture which needs to involve other variables such as the energy consumption and cost. Strangely enough, this wider picture is usually not analyzed in the quantum finance literature.
open_questions.location: Page 20, paragraph starting 'We are here implicitly referring...'

open_questions.question: Can quantum algorithms for PDEs in finance provide a practical advantage over classical methods?
open_questions.quote: An area that is also showing some interesting results is the solution of PDEs using quantum computers with applications to derivative pricing and risk management. While exciting, these approaches have not yet been able to prove whether quantum algorithms can provide an advantage over their classical counterparts.

open_questions.question: How can tensor network methods be extended to encode general empirical data-based probability distributions for finance?
open_questions.quote: Although being a promising method, the extension to a general empirical data-based probability is not, to our knowledge, yet known and needs further research.

open_questions.question: How can we rigorously guarantee performance and speed-up for variational methods used in financial state loading?
open_questions.quote: In general, variational methods do not provide a clear path to get the sought for speed-up. Specifically, it is difficult to guarantee the loading performance by means of rigorous bounds.

open_questions.question: How can quantum advantage for machine learning algorithms in finance be rigorously quantified?
open_questions.quote: Quantifying quantum advantage for ML algorithms is however not straightforward and should be approached carefully.

Para tanto, após uma breve introdução aos conceitos básicos em computação quântica, focaremos nossa atenção na solução baseada no QAOA [25, 58].

key_claims.claim: Quantum finance is a growing research area with increasing scientific publications and startups.
key_claims.quote: Essa nova linha de pesquisa, chamada quantum ﬁnance, tem tido um número crescente de artigos cientíﬁcos [36, 44] e até mesmo o sur- gimento de startups focadas na área como, por exemplo, a DualQ [45] e a Multiverse [46].

key_claims.claim: The urgent challenge in the NISQ era is to demonstrate that quantum algorithms can perform tasks with at least comparable performance to classical computers and to understand when quantum advantage can be expected.
key_claims.quote: Por ora, enquanto o desenvolvimento do hardware não é suﬁciente para ultrapassar a era NISQ, o desaﬁo mais urgente é a prova de princípio de que algoritmos quânti- cos possam executar uma gama de tarefas com desempe- nho ao menos comparável ao dos computadores clássicos e entender sob quais condições vantagens quânticas po- dem ser esperadas.

key_claims.claim: The computational difficulty of portfolio optimization increases substantially when more realistic constraints are added, making it a challenge for modern computational finance.
key_claims.quote: A diﬁculdade computacional que envolve o problema de otimização de portfólio aumenta quando se adicionam restrições (como o da Eq. (28)) mais realistas ao pro- blema. ... Com essas restrições mais realistas, o problema de oti- mização de portfólio pode se tornar substancialmente mais desaﬁador de resolver, mesmo aproximadamente, e é um desaﬁo das ﬁnanças computacionais modernas.
key_claims.location: Page 9, end of Section IV. A. Exemplo prático

key_claims.claim: A variety of quantum algorithmic approaches have been developed to approximately solve constrained portfolio optimization problems.
key_claims.quote: Uma variedade de abordagens algorítmicas quânticas [56, 77– 83] foram desenvolvidas para resolver, ao menos aproxi- madamente, este problema.
key_claims.location: Page 9, end of Section IV. A. Exemplo prático

key_claims.claim: QAOA provides a specific parametrization of quantum states with guarantees of eventual convergence to the optimal value for sufficiently many parameters.
key_claims.quote: O QAOA propõe uma forma especíﬁca de produzir estados quânticos parametrizados com uma garantia de eventual convergência ao valor ótimo do problema para uma quantidade suﬁcientemente grande de parâmetros.
key_claims.location: Page 10, Section V. O ALGORITMO QAOA

key_claims.claim: Due to its simplicity and immediate applicability on early quantum computers, and theoretical guarantees, variational algorithms like QAOA have attracted growing interest.
key_claims.quote: Por sua simplicidade e possibilidade de aplicação imedi- ata nos primeiros computadores quânticos e pelas garan- tias teóricas de convergência e de eﬁciência [44, 77], um crescente interesse da comunidade em algoritmos variaci- onais vem ocorrendo ao longo dos últimos anos [56, 77– 83].
key_claims.location: Page 10, Section V. O ALGORITMO QAOA

key_claims.claim: QAOA pode ser aplicado a problemas de otimização de portfólio formulados como QUBO, retornando soluções consistentes com métodos clássicos.
key_claims.quote: Assim, o resultado da otimização combinatória de portfólio encontrado usando o QAOA é condizente com a carteira ótima encontrada com o método clássico, embora seja válido mencionar novamente que são problemas semelhantes, porém distintos.
key_claims.location: Section V.B. Aplicação à Otimização de Portfólio, Page 14

key_claims.claim: Aumentar o número de camadas p no QAOA tende teoricamente a melhorar a aproximação do valor ótimo, embora na prática haja flutuações.
key_claims.quote: Outro ponto interessante de notar é que o aumento no número de parâmetros usados, implicitamente estabelecido acima como 2p (p valores de γ e p valores de β), tende a melhorar a aproximação do valor ótimo real do problema (embora na prática possam haver ﬂutuações, como mostrado na Fig. 7)...
key_claims.location: Page 11, paragraph starting “Outro ponto interessante de notar...”

key_claims.claim: A amostragem eficiente da distribuição de saída do QAOA, mesmo para p=1, é considerada difícil de simular classicamente e implicaria colapso da hierarquia polinomial.
key_claims.quote: A vantagem quântica do algoritmo QAOA foi investigada na Ref. [86], onde foi mostrado que a amostragem eﬁciente da distribuição de saída de QAOA, mesmo para o caso de menor profundidade de p = 1, implica no colapso da hierarquia polinomial, um forte indício de que não haja uma simulação clássica eﬁciente deste algoritmo.
key_claims.location: Page 12, paragraph starting “A vantagem quântica do algoritmo QAOA...”

key_claims.claim: A aceleração relativa e a garantia de convergência do QAOA ainda são questões de pesquisa em aberto, e novos algoritmos clássicos podem desafiar vantagens quânticas.
key_claims.quote: Contudo, vale dizer, que a relativa aceleração do algoritmo quântico e a garantia de convergência são questões de pesquisa ainda em aberto. Ou seja, é possível que novos algoritmos clássicos mais eﬁcientes sejam descobertos, bem como classe de problemas onde a convergência dos métodos quânticos é desaﬁada.

key_claims.claim: Métodos variacionais como QAOA têm uma desvantagem conhecida de não extensividade da solução com o tamanho do sistema, embora isso seja menos preocupante em otimização combinatória.
key_claims.quote: Uma desvantagem conhecida dos métodos variacionais, famosa no domínio da química quântica, é a não extensividade da solução com o tamanho do sistema. Dito de outro modo, a energia calculada usando tais ferramentas pode não escalar com o tamanho do sistema [87]. Porém, no domínio da otimização combinatória, este fato não é particularmente preocupante...

key_claims.claim: Com p suficientemente grande, o QAOA pode simular com exatidão uma evolução adiabática e, portanto, garantir convergência ao valor ótimo do problema.
key_claims.quote: A importância da Eq. (47) é a demonstrar que, para um número de iterações do algoritmo QAOA p→∞ , existem parâmetros β′ e γ′, pelo menos em princípio, que permitiriam o algoritmo simular com exatidão uma evolução adiabática. Com isso, e usando que a convergência ao valor ótimo do problema de otimização é garantido pelo teorema adiabático, obtemos uma garantia de que uma otimização adequada dos parâmetros β e γ do QAOA deve também permitir convergência ao valor ótimo do problema.
key_claims.location: Section A. Relação do QAOA com a Computação Adiabática, Page 13

key_claims.claim: O QAOA pode ser mais eficiente que a computação adiabática, pois a otimização de parâmetros pode encontrar boas aproximações com poucas iterações.
key_claims.quote: Consequentemente, o QAOA pode ser mais eﬁciente que a computação adiabática, uma vez que, através da otimização dos parâmetros, possivelmente fugindo da prescrição dada pela evolução adiabática, podemos encontrar boas aproximações para o problema de otimização com poucas iterações do QAOA.
key_claims.location: Section A. Relação do QAOA com a Computação Adiabática, Page 13

key_claims.claim: O desempenho do QAOA depende fortemente do otimizador clássico utilizado para ajustar os parâmetros variacionais.
key_claims.quote: Cabe mencionar que a qualidade da solução obtida por meio do QAOA para um determinado problema depende da performance do otimizador clássico usado para otimizar os parâmetros variacionais.
key_claims.location: Section V.B. Aplicação à Otimização de Portfólio, Page 14

key_claims.claim: O comportamento da probabilidade de encontrar o estado ótimo no QAOA em função do número de camadas não é monotônico; mais camadas nem sempre melhoram a solução.
key_claims.quote: Note que o comportamento não é monotônico, ou seja, aumentar o número de camadas nem sempre melhora a probabilidade associada ao vetor |1001⟩ ser a solução ideal.
key_claims.location: Section V.B. Aplicação à Otimização de Portfólio, discussion of Fig. 7, Page 14

key_claims.claim: Há projeção de demonstração de supremacia quântica baseada no QAOA quando computadores com cerca de 420 qubits com correção de erros estiverem disponíveis.
key_claims.quote: Muito embora as limitações do método, há uma projeção de que uma demonstração de supremacia quântica baseada no QAOA assim que um computador quântico de 420 qubits (com correção de erros) esteja disponível [88].
key_claims.location: Page 12, end of paragraph on variational methods

key_claims.claim: O artigo fornece provas de princípio da aplicação do QAOA à otimização de portfólios com um problema simples de 4 ativos.
key_claims.quote: Não só expusemos de forma concisa os principais conceitos, mas também fornecemos provas de princípio desta aplicação, considerando um problema simples com 4 ativos disponíveis na bolsa brasileira.

maturity_indicators.quote:
Ainda que o avanço experimental para criar tais dis- positivos possa levar décadas de pesquisa, a era NISQ
3
... já é uma realidade. Algo que tem motivado uma variedade de novos algoritmos para os quais pode-se garantir o desempenho na presença de erros e assim atingir vantangens computacionais [24].
Na própria RBEF, há diversos tutori- ais explicando como usar circuitos para implementar al- goritmos quânticos no computador quântico da empresa IBM [47–51].
Para este artigo, o QAOA foi implementado através do ATOS Quantum Learning Machine (QLM) [94] que é um ambiente de teste para a computação quântica...
O dispositivo é capaz de simular até 35 qubits e inclui a simulação de ruídos, emulando a arquitetura de computadores quânticos reais.
Fazendo uso do Jupyter Notebook disponível na Ref. [59], pode-se realizar extensivas simulações e, até mesmo, adaptar livremente o código para problemas de seu interesse.

A importância da Eq. (47) é a demonstrar que, para um número de iterações do algoritmo QAOA p→∞ , existem parâmetros β′ e γ′, pelo menos em princípio, que permitiriam o algoritmo simular com exatidão uma evolução adiabática.
maturity_indicators.location: Section A. Relação do QAOA com a Computação Adiabática, Page 13

open_questions.question: Qual é a aceleração relativa real do QAOA em relação a algoritmos clássicos e em quais condições sua convergência é garantida?
open_questions.quote: Contudo, vale dizer, que a relativa aceleração do algoritmo quântico e a garantia de convergência são questões de pesquisa ainda em aberto.

open_questions.question: Podem ser descobertos novos algoritmos clássicos mais eficientes ou classes de problemas em que a convergência dos métodos quânticos é desafiada?
open_questions.quote: Ou seja, é possível que novos algoritmos clássicos mais eﬁcientes sejam descobertos, bem como classe de problemas onde a convergência dos métodos quânticos é desaﬁada.

open_questions.question: Como diferentes otimizadores clássicos afetam a qualidade das soluções do QAOA para problemas financeiros como otimização de portfólio?
open_questions.quote: Entretanto, foge ao escopo desse artigo comparar as soluções obtidas com distintos otimizadores como, por exemplo, COBYLA, BOBYQA, Nelder-Mead, SLSQP, SPSA, entre outros [93].
open_questions.location: Section V.B. Aplicação à Otimização de Portfólio, Page 14

problem_domains.description: Pricing derivatives such as options and collateralized debt obligations using stochastic models and numerical methods.
problem_domains.quote: describing how these solutions, adapted to work on a quantum computer, can potentially help to solve ﬁnancial problems, such as derivative pricing, risk modeling, portfolio optimization, natural language processing, and fraud detection, more eﬃciently and accurately.

problem_domains.description: Computation of risk metrics like VaR, CVaR, economic capital, Greeks, and credit value adjustments under stochastic uncertainty.
problem_domains.quote: such as derivative pricing, risk model- ing, portfolio optimization, natural language processing, and fraud detection, more eﬃciently and accurately.

problem_domains.problem: Value at Risk and Conditional Value at Risk computation
problem_domains.description: Computing VaR and CVaR required by Basel III regulations using stochastic models and Monte Carlo methods.
problem_domains.quote: These regulations require computing numerous risk metrics, such as value at risk (VaR) and conditional value at risk (CVaR). Because of the stochastic nature of the parameters involved in these computations, closed-form analytical solutions are generally not available, and hence numerical methods have to be employed.

problem_domains.problem: Regulatory risk metrics under Basel III
problem_domains.description: Meeting Basel III requirements on capital and risk coverage by computing complex risk metrics efficiently.
problem_domains.quote: Basel III sets requirements on capital, risk coverage, leverage, risk management and supervision, market discipline, liquidity, and supervisory monitoring [11]. These regulations require computing numerous risk metrics, such as value at risk (VaR) and conditional value at risk (CVaR).

problem_domains.description: Analyzing large-scale customer and market data to provide personalized financial services and big-data-driven products.
problem_domains.quote: Customer personalization has become increasingly important in ﬁnance. For example, ﬁnancial technology (Fin- Tech), in contrast to traditional ﬁnance, thrives on providing personalized services.

problem_domains.description: Handling computationally demanding matrix operations arising in financial data analysis.

problem_domains.problem: Cybersecurity and data security in financial services

problem_domains.quote: Ensuring data security is one of the most pressing concerns for the ﬁnancial services industry, according to an article by McKinsey [15] discussing rising cybersecurity issues.

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum Monte Carlo Integration (QMCI) using Quantum Amplitude Estimation
solution_approaches.description: Use QAE to estimate expectations in Monte Carlo integration with quadratically improved error scaling compared to classical Monte Carlo.
solution_approaches.quote: Quantum MCI (QMCI) [150–152] provides a quadratic speedup for Monte Carlo integration by making use of the QAE algorithm (Section 4.4).

solution_approaches.approach: QAE-based Monte Carlo integration procedure
solution_approaches.description: Construct unitaries to load path distributions and payoff functions, then apply QAE to estimate expectations.
solution_approaches.quote:
The task is to computeE[f(ω)] [152], which can be achieved with QAE in three steps as follows.
1. Construct a unitary operatorPl to load a discretized and truncated version ofp(ω)...
2. Convert f into a normalized function˜f : Ω↦→ [0, 1], and construct a unitaryPf that computes ˜f(ω)...
3. Using the notation from Section 4.4, perform quantum amplitude estimation with U =PfPl and an oracle, Oφ, that marks states with the last qubit being|1⟩.

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum-enhanced Multilevel Monte Carlo (quantum MLMC)
solution_approaches.description: Use QMCI as a subroutine within MLMC to approximately recover QMCI error scaling for discretized SDE simulations.
solution_approaches.quote: An et al. [165] proposed a quantum-enhanced version of MLMC that utilizes QMCI as subroutine to compute all expectations involved. This allowed them to approximately recover the error scaling of QMCI, and the approach beneﬁts from being applicable to a wider variety of stochastic dynamics beyond GBM and LV.

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum circuits for simulating local volatility (LV) model
solution_approaches.description: Quantum circuits implementing arithmetic for simulating LV SDE dynamics and state preparation for paths.
solution_approaches.quote: Kaneko et al. [162] proposed quantum circuits implementing the required arithmetic for simulating the LV model, namely, the operationPl, based on improved techniques for simulating stochastic dynamics on a quantum device [163].

solution_approaches.approach: Variational methods for loading distributions (e.g., normal distributions) for GBM
solution_approaches.description: Use variational quantum circuits to prepare distributions like normal distributions, then map to GBM via quantum arithmetic.
solution_approaches.quote: Additionally, variational methods (Section 4.7) have been developed to load distributions [159], such as normal distributions [154]. Geometric Brownian motion (GBM) is an example of a diﬀusion process whose solution is a series of log-normal random variables. These variables can be implemented by utilizing procedures for loading standard normal distributions, followed by quantum arithmetic [154, 155].

solution_approaches.description: Use quantum linear system algorithms to solve linear systems arising from discretized PDEs/ODEs that model financial quantities.
solution_approaches.quote: Because of the linear nature of QLS, QLSAs have been used to solve linear PDEs and ODEs [174–178].

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum finite volume and finite element methods
solution_approaches.description: Amplitude-encoded quantum states combined with FVM/FEM discretizations and QLSA to solve PDEs.
solution_approaches.quote: Similarly, quantum versions of FVM [180] and FEM [178] also use amplitude-encoded quantum states to represent the solution or the basis functions used to approximate the solution, and generate the matrixA based on the relation of the grid points as deﬁned by diﬀerential equations and the respective methods.

solution_approaches.approach: Carleman-linearization-based QLSA for nonlinear ODEs
solution_approaches.description: Approximate nonlinear ODEs via Carleman linearization and solve resulting linear systems with QLSA.
solution_approaches.quote: Speciﬁcally, Liu et al. [183] utilize Carleman linearization to convert dissipative quardratic ODEs into linear ODEs, which are then solved by QLSA.

solution_approaches.approach: Nonlinear ODE/PDE solvers via multiple quantum state copies and linear transformations
solution_approaches.description: Simulate nonlinearities by operating on multiple copies of the quantum state and tracing out extra copies.
solution_approaches.quote: Another approach for implementing nonlinearity is to build multiple copies of the quantum state representing the solution, apply linear transformations in the expanded space to simulate the nonlinearities in the diﬀerential equations, and then trace out the additional copies to achieve the eﬀective nonlinear transformation on a single copy of the quantum state [184, 185].

solution_approaches.approach: Koopman–von Neumann linearization with QLSA
solution_approaches.description: Convert nonlinear ODEs to linear transport PDEs via Koopman–von Neumann formalism and solve with QLSA-based PDE solvers.
solution_approaches.quote: Speciﬁcally, Jin et al. [187] showed that a system ofd nonlinear ODEs can be exactly converted into a d + 1 dimensional linear transport PDE, which can be solved with QLSA-based linear PDE solvers.

solution_approaches.approach: Variational quantum imaginary time evolution (VarQITE) for PDEs
solution_approaches.description: Map PDEs to Wick-rotated Schrödinger equations and solve along imaginary time using variational imaginary-time evolution.
solution_approaches.quote: One approach is to transform the PDE to a Wick-rotated Schrödinger equation with an imaginary time variable and then use variational quantum imaginary time evolution (VarQITE; see Section 6.1.4) to solve the equation along the imaginary time axis. This approach has been demonstrated in solving linear PDEs such as the Black–Scholes equation [189], the Feynman–Kac equation, and the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck equation [190], and nonlinear PDEs such as the Hamilton-Jacobi and the Bellman equation [190].

solution_approaches.approach: Variational circuit ansatz with tensor-network evaluation for PDEs
solution_approaches.description: Use a variational circuit to represent the solution state, implement nonlinearities via multiple copies, and optimize parameters via tensor-network-evaluated cost functions.
solution_approaches.quote: In another approach proposed by Lubasch et al. [191], a variational circuit is built to construct the quantum state representing the solution of the PDE in an amplitude encoding. Nonlinearities are implemented by creating multiple copies of the variational circuit and hence the quantum state. The algorithm then employs tensor net- works to eﬃciently calculate the linear operations acting on the solution functions, and the variational parameters are optimized based on cost functions built on the expectations of these linear operators on the quantum state, obtained by measurements at the end of the circuit.

solution_approaches.approach: Differentiable quantum circuit approach for PDEs and SDE quantile functions
solution_approaches.description: Encode variables via quantum feature maps, define solution as expectation of an operator, and use circuit differentiation to enforce PDE constraints.
solution_approaches.quote:
Quantum circuits in this approach start with a quantum feature map in which values of the function variablesx are used as rotation angles in the circuit. The feature map is followed by a variational circuit parameterized byθ, which produces the quantum state|uθ(x)⟩. The encoded function valueu(x) is then given by the expectation value of a cost operatorC, namely,
u(x) =⟨uθ(x)|C| uθ(x)⟩ .

solution_approaches.approach: VarQITE for trinomial-tree SDE models
solution_approaches.description: Represent trinomial-tree evolution as a Schrödinger equation with non-Hermitian Hamiltonian and simulate with VarQITE to compute expectations.
solution_approaches.quote: Kubo et al. [197] considered the trinomial-tree model [198] for SDEs. The evolution of the probability distribution can be represented as the solution to the Schrödinger equation with a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian and thus simulated with VarQITE. The authors also proposed methods for computing expectation values of functions of the SDE variables.

key_claims.claim: Quantum versions of stochastic modeling, optimization, and machine learning can potentially solve key financial problems more efficiently and accurately.
key_claims.quote: describing how these solutions, adapted to work on a quantum computer, can potentially help to solve ﬁnancial problems, such as derivative pricing, risk model- ing, portfolio optimization, natural language processing, and fraud detection, more eﬃciently and accurately.

key_claims.claim: Many financial problems are relatively tolerant to imprecisions in solutions, making them suitable for near-term quantum computers.

key_claims.location: Section 2.2 Financial Use Cases for Quantum Computing (Page 6)

key_claims.claim: Quantum supremacy has been demonstrated for a specific non-useful task, but quantum advantage for useful large-scale financial problems has not yet been achieved.
key_claims.quote: Thus,quantum supremacy has been achieved. As deﬁned by John Preskill [31], quantum supremacy is the promise that certain computational (not necessarily useful) tasks can be executed exponentially faster on a quantum processor than on a classical one. The decisive demonstration of quantum devices to solve more useful problems faster and/or more accurately than classical computers, such as large-scale ﬁnancial problems (Section 2.2), is calledquantum advantage. Quantum advantage is more elusive and, arguably, has not been demonstrated yet.

key_claims.claim: Current quantum hardware is in the NISQ era, underpowered and suffering from multiple issues, so many algorithms cannot yet show decisive advantage.
key_claims.quote: Current quantum hardware (Section 3.3) is in thenoisy intermediate-scale quantum(NISQ) technology era [32], meaning that the current quantum devices are underpowered and suﬀer from multiple issues.

key_claims.claim: None of the discussed algorithms implemented on NISQ devices arguably provide a decisive advantage over classical algorithms yet.
key_claims.quote: One should keep in mind that arguably none of the discussed algorithms implemented on NISQ devices provide a decisive advantage over classical algorithms yet.

key_claims.claim: Quantum computing may enable computations that are infeasible for current classical computers in reasonable time, leading to unprecedented scalability and accuracy in finance.
key_claims.quote: This promised eﬃciency of quantum computers enables certain computations that are otherwise infeasible for current classical computers to complete in any reasonable amount of time (Section 3).

key_claims.claim: The industry needs to understand which problems can best benefit from quantum computing and the extent of these benefits to fully exploit future production-grade devices.
key_claims.quote: The industry needs to understand the problems that can best beneﬁt from quantum computing and the extent of these beneﬁts, in order to make full use of its revolutionary power when production-grade quantum devices are available.

key_claims.claim: Financial institutions are turning to quantum computing because of its promise to analyze vast amounts of data and compute results faster and more accurately than classical computers.
key_claims.quote: For this reason, several ﬁnancial institutions are turning to quantum computing, given its promise to analyze vast amounts of data and compute results faster and more accurately than any classical computer has ever been able to do.
key_claims.location: Section 2 Applicability of Quantum Computing to Finance (Page 5)

key_claims.claim: QAE-based QMCI achieves error scaling O(1/Nq) compared to O(1/√Ns) for classical Monte Carlo.
Classical PDE/ODE solvers suffer from exponential scaling in dimension, whereas quantum algorithms can potentially achieve polylogarithmic scaling.
key_claims.quote: Speciﬁcally, these algorithms have complexities that scale at least linearly with the number of pointsN on which the solution is to be evaluated and exponentially in the number of dimensionsd of the spatial variable. On the other hand, quantum algorithms often address the same problem by representing a vector of sizeN using O(log N) space, and operating on it in potentiallyO(poly(log N)) time.
key_claims.location: Section 5.2 Numerical Solutions of Differential Equations, Page 18

key_claims.claim: QLSA-based PDE solvers can achieve complexity polynomial in dimension and logarithmic in error tolerance, representing an exponential improvement in dimension.
key_claims.quote: The resultant linear system can then be solved by QLSAs. This approach will potentially give the PDE solver algorithm a complexity of O(poly(d, log(1/ϵ))), where ϵ is the error tolerance, which is an exponential improvement ind compared with that of the best-known classical algorithms.

key_claims.claim: Quantum algorithms for nonlinear ODEs/PDEs often only yield an advantage when many initial data points are involved.
key_claims.quote: Although this approach applies generally to all nonlinear ODEs, it was shown that the only possible quantum advantage one may get in the general case is when we have multiple (M≫ 1) initial data points on which an ensemble average of some physical variables are to be estimated.

key_claims.claim: State preparation and qRAM issues can negate the quadratic speedup of QMCI when classical numerical integration is used.
key_claims.quote: However, it has been shown that when numerical methods such as classical MCI are used to integrate the distribution, QMCI does not provide a quadratic speedup when using this state preparation technique [158].

key_claims.claim: Realizing quantum advantage for QMCI under fault tolerance requires further advances in quantum error correction.
key_claims.quote: Furthermore, if fault tolerance (Section 3) is to be taken into account, advancements in the ﬁeld of quantum error correction are required in order to realize quantum advantage [167].

key_claims.claim: QLSA-based algorithms typically only provide quantum states as outputs, limiting classical access to full solutions but allowing efficient extraction of certain statistics.
key_claims.quote: We note that in all of the QLSA-based algorithms discussed above, the output will be in the form of a quantum state, which is generally diﬃcult to be accessed classically without losing information or voiding the overall quantum speedup. Nevertheless, as discussed in Section 4.5, one can still eﬃciently obtain certain statistics of the solution without classical access to the quantum output state.

key_claims.claim: Problems using variational quantum algorithms are seen as leading potential applications of near-term quantum computing.
key_claims.quote: Problems using VQAs are seen as one of the leading potential applications of near-term quantum computing.

key_claims.claim: QMCI/QAE can justify and accelerate Monte Carlo-based derivative pricing under risk-neutral measures.
key_claims.quote: Thus, the value of the derivative at t, Vt, is equal E[C(t, T)|Ft]. This justiﬁes the usage of MCI for derivative pricing [12, 200], assuming sample paths follow the risk-neutral measure... Pricing of more complicated derivatives with QAE can be found in the literature.

The authors avoided this issue by reading out the expected value of the option at a future time point... This approach results in an exponential speedup in terms of the dimension of the PDE over the classical FDM-based approach.

key_claims.quote: The expected total loss E[L] can be eﬃciently computed classically, so only the estimate of VaRα[L] is computed by using QAE [216].

key_claims.claim: Quantum annealers currently have limited connectivity, making embedding arbitrary QUBOs difficult and heuristic.
key_claims.quote: These devices have limited connectivity resulting in extra qubits being needed to encode arbitrary QUBO problems (i.e., Ising models with interactions at arbitrary distances). key_claims.location: Page 25, paragraph starting 'The D-Wave devices are examples of commercially available quantum annealers...'

key_claims.claim: Quantum linear systems methods can provide exponential speedup for relaxed convex portfolio optimization when only partial information about the solution is required.
key_claims.quote: Thus, if only partial information about the solution is required, QLS methods potentially provide an exponential speedup, inN, over all known classical algorithms for this scenario, although the sparsity and well-conditioned matrix assumptions mentioned in Section 4.5 have to be met to obtain this speedup.

key_claims.claim: Quantum annealing enables solving large QUBO formulations of swap netting problems in parallel for each subset of swaps.
key_claims.quote: Rosenberg et al. [306] formulated the task of ﬁnding a set of “nettable” swaps associated with a single counterparty that maximizes the total notional value as a QUBO. This optimization problem can be solved in parallel for each subset of potentially nettable swaps. ... The QUBO problems were solved by utilizing quantum annealing (Section 6.1.1).

key_claims.claim: Formulating optimal currency arbitrage as a QUBO and solving via quantum annealing addresses an NP-hard problem.
key_claims.quote: Soon and Ye [315] formulated the task of identifying the optimal currency arbitrage opportunity in the graph structure mentioned above as a binary linear programming problem. Thus this problem isNP-hard (Section 6.1). Rosenberg [313] reformulated this as a QUBO and solved it using quantum annealing.

key_claims.claim: Counting institutional failures in financial networks is NP-hard, but mapping to QUBO and solving with quantum methods can help analyze crash propagation.
key_claims.quote: Elliot et al. [317] developed a problem formulation for counting the number of intuitions that fail in a ﬁnancial network. Their proposed problem was found to beNP-hard [318]. If solved, however, it allows for analyzing how small changes in the network propagate through a web of complex interdependencies, something that is diﬃcult [319] with alternative techniques for crash prediction [320]. By modeling a ﬁnancial system, mapping the system to a QUBO problem, and perturbing the system to ﬁnd the ground state it reaches, we can determine the eﬀect of small perturbations on the market.

key_claims.claim: Quantum SVMs can achieve logarithmic runtime in the number and dimension of training examples under data-access assumptions.
key_claims.quote: A quantum SVM was ﬁrst proposed by Rebentrost et al. [331], who showed that a quantum SVM can be implemented withO(log M N) runtime in both training and classiﬁcation stages, under the assumption that there are oracles for the training data ... and the states are constructed by using qRAM [70, 332].
