key_claims.claim: Quantum Boltzmann machines implemented via annealing or variational methods can handle more complex graph structures than classical Boltzmann machines.
key_claims.quote: Quantum Boltzmann machines have been implemented by utilizing quantum annealing (Section 6.1.1) [379–381]. ... Since quantum states are always normalized, this approach allows for implementing Boltzmann machines with more complex graph structures.

key_claims.claim: Quantum generative adversarial networks may exhibit exponential advantage over classical GANs when learning from high-dimensional measurement data.

key_claims.claim: Quantum machine learning for finance is still immature and may take decades to yield practical applications, despite its promise.
key_claims.quote: Such models face many challenges, however, such as trainability, accuracy, and eﬃciency, that need to be addressed in order to maintain the hope of achieving quantum advantage when scaling up these near-term quantum devices [130]. Substantial eﬀorts are needed before we can answer the question of whether quantum machine learning algorithms can bring us practical and useful applications, and it might take decades.

key_claims.claim: Quantum-enhanced anomaly detection methods (GANs, amplitude estimation, clustering, Boltzmann machines) are promising for financial fraud detection.
key_claims.quote: Researchers have also proposed quantum versions of these approaches, such as quantum GANs (Section 7.6). ... Quantum amplitude estimation (Section 4.4) was utilized to enhance density-estimation- based anomaly detection [441]. Quantum variants of common clustering methods also exist, such ask-means (Section 7.3), that could be useful for anomaly detection. ... Quantum Boltzmann machines (Section 7.5.3) have also been used for fraud detection [273].

key_claims.claim: Quantum LSTM-like models may offer advantages over classical models for asset pricing in terms of training complexity and prediction performance.
key_claims.quote: Both make use of parameterized quantum circuits, and these QML models may oﬀer an advantage over classical models in terms of training complexity and prediction performance.

key_claims.quote: Quantum-accelerated multilevel monte carlo methods for stochastic diﬀerential equations in mathematical ﬁnance. Quantum, 5:481, June 2021.

metadata.title: CryptoQNet: Leveraging Quantum Computing for Enhanced Cryptocurrency Market Analysis
metadata.venue: 2025 International Conference on Emerging Smart Computing and Informatics (ESCI)

problem_domains.description: The paper targets accurate analysis and forecasting of highly volatile and nonlinear cryptocurrency markets, focusing on Bitcoin and Ethereum.
problem_domains.quote: Cryptocurrency markets are characterized by high volatility and nonlinear dynamics, making accurate analysis and forecasting challenging.

problem_domains.description: The work focuses on predicting Bitcoin and Ethereum prices and evaluating prediction errors.
problem_domains.quote: CryptoQNet outperforms classical models such as LSTMs and GRUs, achieving a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 0.021 and Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) of 0.028 for Bitcoin price predictions... For Ethereum, the model achieved an MAE of 0.018 and RMSE of 0.025, demonstrating its robustness in modeling complex market trends.

problem_domains.description: The model is designed to predict cryptocurrency market volatility and reduce volatility-related prediction errors.
problem_domains.quote: Additionally, CryptoQNet significantly reduced Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) for volatility prediction, achieving 3.2% for Bitcoin and 3.6% for Ethereum, compared to over 5% by classical models.

problem_domains.problem: identifying key market drivers / feature importance
problem_domains.description: The study aims to identify which features (e.g., price, volume) are most influential in cryptocurrency market trends.
problem_domains.quote: The model also provides enhanced interpretability, identifying price and volume as key factors influencing market trends.

problem_domains.problem: balancing trading profits and energy costs in cryptocurrency trading and mining
problem_domains.description: The paper discusses optimizing both financial returns and energy costs, particularly in Bitcoin mining and trading strategies.
problem_domains.quote: CryptoQNet, a quantum-inspired multi-objective optimization framework designed to optimize both trading profits and energy costs. By integrating quantum computing concepts, CryptoQNet offers a powerful approach to balancing financial and energy objectives, crucial for operations like Bitcoin mining.

problem_domains.description: The framework aims to optimize trading strategies and decision-making to manage volatility and profitability in cryptocurrency markets.
problem_domains.quote: By leveraging quantum-inspired optimization techniques, CryptoQNet aims to optimize trading strategies and improve decision-making, offering new insights for managing market volatility and profitability in the evolving cryptocurrency landscape.

problem_domains.problem: scalability and high-dimensional data in cryptocurrency forecasting
problem_domains.description: The paper addresses the difficulty classical models have with volatile, high-dimensional cryptocurrency data and scalability.
problem_domains.quote: Cryptocurrency market analysis have explored traditional machine learning models and deep learning techniques to predict market trends, yet these methods often struggle with the complexities of volatile and high-dimensional data.

problem_domains.problem: limitations of classical models (LSTM, GRU, etc.) for cryptocurrency forecasting
problem_domains.description: The work responds to the shortcomings of LSTM, GRU, and other classical models in handling volatility, rapid fluctuations, and computational demands.
problem_domains.quote: Previous studies have explored traditional machine learning models like LSTM and GRU on datasets such as historical cryptocurrency prices and social media sentiment, yet they struggle with the volatile and high-dimensional nature of the data.

problem_domains.problem: optimizing trading strategies and trading efficiency
problem_domains.description: The study targets improving trading strategy optimization and trading efficiency in cryptocurrency markets.
problem_domains.quote: This paper aims to address these gaps by applying quantum machine learning techniques, like Quantum Neural Networks, to cryptocurrency market analysis, improving prediction accuracy and trading efficiency [17].

problem_domains.problem: computational inefficiency and scalability in high-dimensional, volatile financial data
problem_domains.description: The paper addresses computational inefficiency and scalability issues of deep learning models on high-dimensional, volatile cryptocurrency data.
problem_domains.quote: However, these models struggle with computational inefficiency, market non-stationarity, and inconsistent performance during high volatility. This paper introduces CryptoQNet, leveraging Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs) to address these gaps by enhancing computational speed and prediction robustness in cryptocurrency analysis [20].

problem_domains.problem: securing and analyzing digital assets in the quantum era
problem_domains.description: The framework is also positioned as addressing security and analysis of digital assets against quantum-era threats.
problem_domains.quote: By addressing vulnerabilities in traditional cryptographic methods and enabling quantum-resilient strategies, CryptoQNet provides a robust framework for securing and analyzing digital assets.

problem_domains.problem: cryptocurrency market analysis and volatility prediction (formal objective)
problem_domains.description: One explicit objective is to design and implement a quantum computing framework for cryptocurrency market analysis and volatility prediction.
problem_domains.quote: To design and implement CryptoQNet, a quantum computing framework tailored for cryptocurrency market analysis and volatility prediction.

problem_domains.problem: forecasting cryptocurrency price trends and identifying key market drivers
problem_domains.description: Another explicit objective is forecasting price trends and identifying key drivers using an interpretable and computationally efficient model.
problem_domains.quote: To explore the interpretability and computational efficiency of the proposed model in forecasting cryptocurrency price trends and identifying key market drivers.

solution_approaches.approach: CryptoQNet quantum computing-based model
solution_approaches.description: A novel quantum computing-based model integrating several quantum components to improve cryptocurrency market analysis and forecasting.
solution_approaches.quote: This study proposes a novel quantum computing-based model, CryptoQNet, to address these challenges by leveraging Quantum Feature Maps, Variational Quantum Circuits, and Quantum Recurrent Neural Networks.

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum Feature Maps
solution_approaches.description: Quantum Feature Maps are used to map classical cryptocurrency data into a high-dimensional Hilbert space to enhance feature separability.
solution_approaches.quote: This study presents CryptoQNet, a quantum computing framework that leverages Quantum Feature Maps, Variational Quantum Circuits, and Quantum Recurrent Neural Networks to analyze cryptocurrency trends, enhancing data representation and prediction accuracy for price movements and market volatility

solution_approaches.approach: Variational Quantum Circuit (VQC)
solution_approaches.description: A trainable variational quantum circuit processes encoded data, with parameters optimized via classical optimizers using the parameter-shift rule.
solution_approaches.quote: The encoded data is processed using a Variational Quantum Circuit (VQC), which consists of trainable parameters optimized during the learning process.

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum Recurrent Neural Network (QRNN)
solution_approaches.description: A quantum variant of LSTM is used to capture temporal dependencies in cryptocurrency time-series forecasting.
solution_approaches.quote: For time-series forecasting, we extend CryptoQNet with a Quantum Recurrent Neural Network (QRNN). The QRNN incorporates temporal dependencies using a quantum variant of the LSTM architecture.
solution_approaches.location: Methodology – Quantum Recurrent Neural Network (QRNN), Page 3

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum Data Preprocessing with Amplitude Encoding
solution_approaches.description: Historical cryptocurrency data is normalized and encoded into quantum states using amplitude encoding.
solution_approaches.quote: The dataset, consisting of historical prices, volumes, and other features of Bitcoin and Ethereum, is preprocessed and encoded into quantum states using Amplitude Encoding .

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum Feature Engineering via Quantum Feature Maps
solution_approaches.description: Classical data is mapped to a high-dimensional Hilbert space using a parameterized unitary feature map.
solution_approaches.quote: To enhance feature separability, Quantum Feature Maps (QFM) are applied. The classical data is mapped to a high-dimensional Hilbert space H using a feature map φ(x).

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum Optimization with hybrid quantum-classical training
solution_approaches.description: Training uses a quantum circuit with classical optimizers (Adam, RMSProp) and parameter-shift gradients to minimize cross-entropy loss.
solution_approaches.quote: The optimization is performed using a classical optimizer such as Adam or RMSProp. The gradient of the loss with respect to the parameters is computed using the parameter-shift rule:

solution_approaches.approach: quantum-inspired multi-objective optimization framework
solution_approaches.description: CryptoQNet is described as a quantum-inspired multi-objective optimization framework to optimize trading profits and energy costs.
solution_approaches.quote: CryptoQNet, a quantum-inspired multi-objective optimization framework designed to optimize both trading profits and energy costs.

solution_approaches.approach: quantum-inspired optimization techniques for trading strategies
solution_approaches.description: The framework leverages quantum-inspired optimization techniques to optimize trading strategies and decision-making.
solution_approaches.quote: By leveraging quantum-inspired optimization techniques, CryptoQNet aims to optimize trading strategies and improve decision-making, offering new insights for managing market volatility and profitability in the evolving cryptocurrency landscape.

solution_approaches.approach: hybrid quantum-classical optimization (VQC with classical gradients)
solution_approaches.description: The model uses a hybrid approach where quantum circuits are optimized with classical gradient-based methods.
solution_approaches.quote: Hybrid Quantum-Classical Optimization: The variational quantum circuit (VQC) optimization leverages classical gradient-based methods, striking a balance between computational feasibility and quantum enhancements.

problem_solution_mappings.approach: CryptoQNet quantum computing-based model
problem_solution_mappings.quote: This study proposes a novel quantum computing-based model, CryptoQNet, to address these challenges by leveraging Quantum Feature Maps, Variational Quantum Circuits, and Quantum Recurrent Neural Networks.

problem_solution_mappings.approach: Quantum Recurrent Neural Network (QRNN

key_claims.claim: CryptoQNet achieves lower prediction errors than classical LSTM and GRU models for Bitcoin and Ethereum price prediction.

key_claims.claim: CryptoQNet significantly reduces MAPE for volatility prediction compared to classical models.
key_claims.quote: Additionally, CryptoQNet significantly reduced Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) for volatility prediction, achieving 3.2% for Bitcoin and 3.6% for Ethereum, compared to over 5% by classical models.

key_claims.claim: CryptoQNet provides enhanced interpretability by identifying price and volume as key factors influencing market trends.
key_claims.quote: The model also provides enhanced interpretability, identifying price and volume as key factors influencing market trends.

key_claims.claim: Despite higher training time due to quantum computations, CryptoQNet offers efficient inference and high accuracy, making it promising for financial forecasting.
key_claims.quote: While training time is higher due to quantum computations, inference efficiency and accuracy make CryptoQNet a promising tool for financial forecasting.

key_claims.claim: Quantum computing offers transformative potential for financial systems, enabling faster and more accurate market analysis, risk assessment, and fraud detection.

key_claims.claim: CryptoQNet enhances computational speed and prediction robustness in cryptocurrency analysis relative to classical models that suffer from inefficiency and non-stationarity.
key_claims.quote: This paper introduces CryptoQNet, leveraging Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs) to address these gaps by enhancing computational speed and prediction robustness in cryptocurrency analysis [20].

key_claims.claim: CryptoQNet consistently demonstrates lower prediction errors across all forecasting horizons, indicating robustness in modeling temporal dependencies.
key_claims.quote: The proposed model consistently demonstrates lower prediction errors across all forecasting horizons, indicating its robustness in modeling temporal dependencies.

key_claims.claim: CryptoQNet significantly outperforms classical models in predicting market volatility, reducing MAPE by a substantial margin.

key_claims.claim: Experiments were conducted on quantum simulators due to limited access to actual quantum hardware, which is a limitation.

key_claims.claim: As dataset size increases, the depth and complexity of quantum circuits may pose scalability challenges.
key_claims.quote: Scalability Concerns: As the dataset size increases, the depth and complexity of quantum circuits may pose challenges. This limitation emphasizes the need for scalable quantum algorithms.

key_claims.claim: The training phase of CryptoQNet incurs higher computational costs than classical models due to quantum circuit evaluations.

key_claims.claim: CryptoQNet’s efficient inference and interpretability make it a promising tool for financial forecasting and risk management despite training overhead.
key_claims.quote: Despite its computational overhead during training, CryptoQNet’s efficient inference phase and interpretability make it a promising tool for financial forecasting and risk management.

maturity_indicators.quote: The experiments were conducted on quantum simulators due to limited access to actual quantum hardware.

This study presents CryptoQNet, a quantum computing framework that leverages Quantum Feature Maps, Variational Quantum Circuits, and Quantum Recurrent Neural Networks to analyze cryptocurrency trends, enhancing data representation and prediction accuracy for price movements and market volatility

Future work will focus on deploying the model on real-world quantum hardware, integrating external data sources, and exploring hybrid quantum-classical architectures to further enhance its scalability and applicability in dynamic financial environments.

open_questions.question: How will CryptoQNet perform when deployed on real-world quantum hardware, considering noise and decoherence?
open_questions.quote: Real-World Quantum Hardware Testing: Testing CryptoQNet on quantum hardware will provide deeper insights into its practical applicability and address potential hardware-specific challenges such as noise and decoherence.

open_questions.question: How can external factors like social media sentiment, macroeconomic indicators, and global news be integrated to enhance forecasting?
open_questions.quote: Integration with External Factors: Incorporating social media sentiment, macroeconomic indicators, and global news data can enhance the model’s forecasting capabilities.

open_questions.question: Can CryptoQNet be extended to portfolio optimization for multi-asset cryptocurrency portfolios?
open_questions.quote: Portfolio Optimization: Extending CryptoQNet to analyze and optimize multi-asset cryptocurrency portfolios can provide more comprehensive insights for investors.

open_questions.question: How can hybrid quantum-classical architectures (e.g., with transformers) further improve predictive accuracy and scalability?
open_questions.quote: Hybrid Quantum-Classical Models: Exploring hybrid architectures that combine quantum computing with advanced classical models such as transformers may further enhance predictive accuracy and scalability.

problem_domains.problem: Finance as a domain of optimization problems
problem_domains.description: Finance is identified as a rich source of optimization problems that can be used to benchmark and eventually validate the real-world impact of quantum optimization.
problem_domains.quote:
Lastly, we highlight two domains – finance and sustainability – as rich
sources of optimization problems that could be used to benchmark, and eventually validate, the
potential real-world impact of quantum optimization.

problem_domains.description: Discussion of quantum speedups and limitations for NP-hard optimization problems, including worst-case vs typical instances and approximation settings.
problem_domains.quote: Although it is widely believed that quantum computers will not offer exponential speedups forNP-hard problems, the story does not end there. As we have seen, most complexity-theoretic statements deal with worst-case settings for exact solutions. In practice, typical optimization problem instances could differ substantially from the worst-case, and thus, exponential quantum speedups in these more realistic settings are still possible in principle.
problem_domains.location: Page 11, Section III.D Takeaways from Complexity Theory in Quantum Optimization

problem_domains.problem: Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP) and shortest path
problem_domains.description: Use of TSP and shortest path as examples of how problem structure and restrictions change complexity and solvability.
problem_domains.quote: A perfect example of this is TSP, which – in its most general decision version form – is bothAPX-hard andNP-hard. If we restrict to Euclidean TSP, where all points are in Rd and edge weights equal their Euclidean distances, then, remarkably, there exists an explicitPTAS to solve such TSP instances [61]. Shifting to heuristic algorithms for TSP, one can actually solve problems in practice with up to millions of variables. Lastly, if we were to consider the shortest path problem instead of TSP, where we just want the shortest path between two places, wewouldhaveaproblemin P.
problem_domains.location: Page 11, Section III.D Takeaways from Complexity Theory in Quantum Optimization

problem_domains.description: Unstructured search and function minimization over combinatorial spaces, framed via Grover search and brute-force baselines.
problem_domains.quote: In exact quantum optimization, this advantage translates to an advantage for function minimization [89] and can achieve a quadratic speedup over brute force search in many problems in combinatorial optimization [93], i.e., a run time of O( √ 2n) instead of O(2n) for n-variable problems.

problem_domains.problem: Ground state problems / Hamiltonian ground state search
problem_domains.description: Optimization framed as finding the ground state of a Hamiltonian corresponding to the optimal solution.
problem_domains.quote: It assumes a problem HamiltonianH whose ground state corresponds to the solution of a corresponding optimization problem, as well as a so-called mixing HamiltonianHX.

problem_domains.quote: Other types of unconstrained discrete optimization problems involve, for instance, high-order polynomial objective functions [179], also referred to as Polynomial Unconstrained Binary Optimization (PUBO), or Blackbox objective functions [180] as well as (bounded) integer variables.

problem_domains.description: MAXCUT as a canonical QUBO / APX-complete problem and target for approximation algorithms and quantum heuristics.
problem_domains.quote: Some problems, such as MAXCUT, can be naturally formulated as a QUBO, and most unconstrained discrete optimization problems can be mapped to QUBOs, for example, by replacing integer variables by a suitable encoding [181] or by converting higher-order polynomial terms to additional binary variables and quadratic terms [182, 183].

problem_domains.problem: Optimal stopping problems / American option pricing
problem_domains.description: Optimal stopping problems including financial derivative pricing, especially American options, involving stochastic modeling and dynamic programming.
problem_domains.quote:
Closely related to MDPs are optimal stopping prob-
lems. These problems are concerned with timing an ac-
tion for maximizing a reward and are often solved with
dynamic programming. Optimal stopping appears, for
example, in sequential parameter estimation [338], se-
quential hypothesis testing [339], and, most famously, in
financial derivative pricing [340]. The pricing of Ameri-
can options involves stochastic modeling of asset prices
and performing a combination of Monte-Carlo estima-
tion, least-squares regression, and dynamic programming
for the optimal stopping time [340].

curacy in optimization and allows to model uncertainty

problem_domains.quote:
The key problem associated with HJB equation, con-
tinuous or discrete, is thecurse of dimensionality. Solv-
ing HJB in Eq. (17) by conventional methods of numer-
ical analysis quickly becomes intractable even in rather
modest dimensions, e.g., ifx(t) ∈ Rn for n ≥ 10.

problem_domains.description: Need for standardized, fair, and reproducible benchmarks to compare classical and quantum optimization approaches.
problem_domains.quote: Optimization competitions and libraries of this form that are compatible with (near-term) quantum computers do not exist as of now. It remains an open task to set them up and, thereby, enable streamlined benchmarking of quantum optimization methods.

problem_domains.problem: comparison of classical and quantum algorithms to demonstrate quantum advantage
problem_domains.description: Establishing problem-centric benchmarks that allow direct comparison of runtimes and solution qualities between classical and quantum solvers.
problem_domains.quote: One of the main goals of benchmarking in the present context is the comparison of classical and quantum algorithms — aiming at demonstrating quantum advantage.

problem_domains.problem: tracking progress in hardware and algorithmic developments
problem_domains.description: Using benchmarks to monitor improvements in quantum hardware, software, and algorithms over time.
problem_domains.quote: Benchmarking may also be executed to track the progress in hardware developments (cf. Sec. VIA) as well as algorithmic improvements.

problem_domains.problem: understanding scaling behavior and phase transitions in optimization problems
problem_domains.description: Analyzing how algorithm performance and resource needs scale with problem size and structure, including phase transitions.
problem_domains.quote: Furthermore, benchmarking can give us insights into an algorithm’s scaling behavior: Is there a problem scale at which algorithms fail to provide good solutions — possibly due to hardware limitations?

problem_domains.description: Deciding whether benchmarks should be defined at the level of original optimization problems or specific mathematical models.
problem_domains.quote: For benchmarks, it is therefore crucial to decide on the level a problem is defined: either model-independent, i.e., on the level of the original optimization problem, which allows different mathematical modeling methods, or model-dependent, i.e., on the level of a concrete mathematical model.

problem_domains.description: Using classical pre-processing to reduce problem size and complexity before applying optimization algorithms.
problem_domains.quote: The goal of pre-processing is to modify the problem in such a way that it allows the optimization algorithm to work more efficiently.

problem_domains.description: Choosing and comparing different classical and quantum hardware platforms for optimization tasks.
problem_domains.quote: Tailoring the choice of platform to the characteristics of the problem at hand – if possible – can lead to better outcomes. This approach aligns with the idea of platform-aware optimization, ensuring that the selected platform is optimally matched to the unique requirements of the problem being addressed.

problem_domains.problem: defining fair metrics for classical vs quantum comparison
problem_domains.description: Selecting resource, runtime, quality, and complexity metrics that allow fair comparison between classical and quantum optimization methods.
problem_domains.quote: Due to the technological differences between classical and quantum systems, the selection of a set of metrics that enable a fair comparison – such as tools for investigating the complexity of a problem and a thorough resource analysis – are crucial.

problem_domains.problem: identifying suitable hard optimization problems for quantum benchmarks
problem_domains.description: Finding problem instances that are hard for state-of-the-art classical solvers but small and structured enough for near-term quantum hardware.
problem_domains.quote: The problems should be chosen sufficiently hard for state-of-the-art classical solvers to leave a margin for quantum methods but within an intermediate size range where current and/or near-term quantum technologies can be effectively deployed.

problem_domains.problem: Maximum Independent Set (MIS) as a benchmark problem

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum optimization algorithms (general)
solution_approaches.description: The work surveys and structures multiple algorithmic approaches for quantum optimization, including exact, approximate, and heuristic methods, and their building blocks.
solution_approaches.quote:
With these aspects in mind, this work draws on multiple approaches to
study quantum optimization. Provably exact versus heuristic settings are first explained using
computational complexity theory — highlighting where quantum advantage is possible in each
context. Then, the core building blocks for quantum optimization algorithms are outlined to
subsequently define prominent problem classes and identify key open questions that, if answered,
will advance the field.

solution_approaches.approach: Grover Search
solution_approaches.description: Use of Grover's algorithm as an exact quantum optimization method providing quadratic speedup for function minimization and combinatorial search.
solution_approaches.quote: The seminal Grover algorithm for searching an unstructured database achieves a quadratic advantage over classical search in terms of the number of queries to the database (i.e. the query complexity). In exact quantum optimization, this advantage translates to an advantage for function minimization [89] and can achieve a quadratic speedup over brute force search in many problems in combinatorial optimization [93].

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum Adiabatic Algorithm (QAA) / quantum annealing
solution_approaches.description: Adiabatic evolution from an easy mixing Hamiltonian to a problem Hamiltonian whose ground state encodes the optimal solution.
solution_approaches.quote: The Quantum Adiabatic Algorithm (QAA) is another exact optimization algorithm, reminiscent of homotopy methods of numerical mathematics [97]. It assumes a problem HamiltonianH whose ground state corresponds to the solution of a corresponding optimization problem, as well as a so-called mixing HamiltonianHX.
solution_approaches.location: Page 11-12, Section III.B Quantum Adiabatic Algorithm

solution_approaches.approach: Diabatic and counter-diabatic annealing
solution_approaches.description: Variants of quantum annealing that relax strict adiabaticity or add counter-diabatic terms to suppress excitations.
solution_approaches.quote: The practical implementation of the quantum annealing protocol often involves repeated finite-time runs [104] or, potentially, diabatic annealing [105]. This variant relaxes the constraint that the system must always remain in the instantaneous ground state ofH(t). Another variant is counter-diabatic annealing, where additional terms are included in the Hamiltonian to suppress the transition to excited states during the annealing [106, 107].
solution_approaches.location: Page 12, Section III.B Quantum Adiabatic Algorithm

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum Phase Estimation (QPE)
solution_approaches.description: Use of QPE to estimate eigenvalues/eigenvectors of Hamiltonians encoding optimization problems, potentially aiding ground state finding.
solution_approaches.quote: Quantum Phase Estimation (QPE) is an algorithm to estimate the eigenphases of unitary operators [111]. It allows the estimation of the eigenvalues of certain matrices and can be used to find the ground state and corresponding energy of various Hamiltonians [112–114].
solution_approaches.location: Page 12, Section III.C Quantum Phase Estimation

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum linear algebra toolbox (quantum signal processing, singular value transformation, block-encoding)
solution_approaches.description: Use of quantum matrix algebra primitives to simulate Hamiltonians, prepare Gibbs states, and solve continuous optimization-related problems.
solution_approaches.quote: Quantum signal processing [129] enables the simulation of sparse matrices, i.e., the implementation of the time evolution operatore−iHt for a matrix H and a timet, with optimal complexity. Phase estimation then allows to extract eigenvalues and eigenvectors of H. Quantum singular value transformation [130] generalizes this result in an optimal way and allows efficient simulation of matrix algebra such asA+ B, AB, and singular value transformationsP (A)... The block-encoding framework unifies input models for matrices... These tools find applications in preparing Gibbs states, matrix problems, and continuous optimization.
solution_approaches.location: Page 12, Section III.C Quantum Phase Estimation

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum Gibbs sampling and Gibbs state preparation
solution_approaches.description: Quantum algorithms (including variational and dissipative methods) to prepare or sample from Gibbs states for use in optimization and SDP/zero-sum game algorithms.
solution_approaches.quote: QuantumGibbssamplingplaysacrucialroleinvarious optimization algorithms, particularly in convex optimization as discussed in Sec. IVB1. Quantum speedups are possible because, under certain conditions, Gibbs states can be prepared more efficiently quantumly than classically.

solution_approaches.approach: Variational Gibbs state preparation (thermofield double, VQA-based)
solution_approaches.description: Variational quantum algorithms to approximate finite-temperature Gibbs states using thermofield double states or truncated Taylor series free-energy objectives.
solution_approaches.quote: A variational method for quantum simulators to generate finite temperature Gibbs states through the preparation of thermofield double states was introduced in [142]... A different VQA approach for the preparation of Gibbs states suitable for NISQ devices was presented in [143] where the authors presented an algorithm in their paper by applying a truncated Taylor series to compute the free energy, and then selecting this truncated value as the loss function.

solution_approaches.approach: Dissipative Quantum Gibbs Sampling
solution_approaches.description: A dissipative algorithm using local update rules for Gibbs sampling, designed to be simpler and more feasible for near-term hardware.
solution_approaches.quote: Additionally, recent advancements in quantum Gibbs sampling, like the Dissipative Quantum Gibbs Sampling algorithm [134], offer a simpler and potentially more efficient alternative, as they utilize local update rules and are more feasible for near-term quantum hardware.

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum SDP solvers (Matrix Multiplicative Weights Update, etc.)
solution_approaches.description: Quantum algorithms for semidefinite programming that leverage Gibbs states and block-encoding to potentially achieve speedups.
solution_approaches.quote: This method and its applications in algorithms like the Matrix Multiplicative Weights Update for solving general semidefinite optimization problems are further elaborated in [147–151]. Notably, these algorithms leverage Gibbs states for computing trace inner products.

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum-accelerated approximation algorithms via SDP relaxations
solution_approaches.description: Use of quantum subroutines to accelerate classical approximation algorithms such as Goemans-Williamson for MAXCUT.
solution_approaches.quote: Quantum Computing could be used to accelerate known classical approximation algorithms via Quantum subroutines. For instance, Semidefinite Programming (SDP) relaxations, as used in the famous Goemans-Williamson algorithm for MAXCUT [163, 164] or more general variants for QUBO [165], may profit from Quantum SDP solvers, cf. Sec. IVB1.

solution_approaches.approach: Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs)
solution_approaches.description: Hybrid quantum-classical schemes that optimize parameters of a quantum ansatz to minimize a cost function related to the optimization problem.
solution_approaches.quote: A family of randomized search algorithms, often termed as Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) [168], decomposes the original optimization problem into solving smaller-scale optimization problems classically and evaluating certain expectations quantumly.

solution_approaches.approach: Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE)
solution_approaches.description: A VQA to approximate ground states of Hamiltonians, used for QUBO/Ising optimization by minimizing the expectation of the problem Hamiltonian.
solution_approaches.quote: Originally proposed for quantum chemistry applications, the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) [186] denotes a class of heuristic VQAs to approximate ground states of Hamiltonians.
solution_approaches.location: Page 16, Section IV.A.1 Unconstrained Discrete Optimization

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA)
solution_approaches.description: A problem-inspired VQE variant using alternating problem and mixing unitaries to approximate solutions to QUBOs like MAXCUT.
solution_approaches.quote: The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) [190] denotes a special case of VQE that can be applied to find good solutions to QUBOs.
solution_approaches.location: Page 16, Section IV.A.1 Unconstrained Discrete Optimization

solution_approaches.approach: Warm-started QAOA
solution_approaches.description: QAOA variants that initialize from classical approximate solutions to improve performance and inherit some guarantees.
solution_approaches.quote: Other variants adjust QAOA in order to warm-start it from solutions obtained by classical algorithms. The idea is to use a classical algorithm to compute an approximate solution, and then use it to warm-start QAOA to further improve upon the obtained solution [177, 178]. These approaches inherit some of the performance guarantees of the classical algorithms used for warm-starting and have been shown to significantly outperform standard QAOA on certain instances.
solution_approaches.location: Page 16-17, Section IV.A.1 Unconstrained Discrete Optimization

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum Alternating Operator Ansatz (constraint-preserving QAOA variants)
solution_approaches.description: QAOA-family ansätze that encode constraints into the mixer so that only feasible states are explored.
solution_approaches.quote: The Quantum Alternating Operator Ansatz, which shares the acronym QAOA, denotes a family of QAOA variants that encode constraints into the mixer such that they are preserved and the algorithm is restricted to feasible states.
solution_approaches.location: Page 16, Section IV.A.1 Unconstrained Discrete Optimization

solution_approaches.approach: Recursive QAOA and recursive quantum approaches
solution_approaches.description: Use of QAOA iteratively to reduce problem size by fixing variables based on estimated correlations, then solving the reduced instance classically.
solution_approaches.quote: Another alternative approach to QAOA is Recursive QAOA [206], which uses the quantum computer to produce a sequence of reduced problems. Here, at each step QAOA is used to estimate correlations between variables, and the problem Hamiltonian is reduced by fixing the strongest one.
solution_approaches.location: Page 17, Section IV.A.1 Unconstrained Discrete Optimization

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum Random Access Optimization (QRAO) / Quantum Relaxation Algorithms
solution_approaches.description: Algorithms that encode more variables than qubits via non-diagonal Hamiltonians and approximate ground states to get MAXCUT approximations.
solution_approaches.quote: Another family of near-term compatible approximation algorithms for MAXCUT is given by Quantum Random Access Optimization (QRAO, also called Quantum Relaxation Algorithms) [215, 216]. Here, the variable-to-qubit ratio is chosen to be larger than one and results in a non-diagonal Hamiltonian.
solution_approaches.location: Page 17, Section IV.A.1 Unconstrained Discrete Optimization

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum Imaginary Time Evolution (QITE) and variational QITE
solution_approaches.description: Imaginary-time evolution to project onto ground states, implemented approximately via variational principles or Taylor expansions.
solution_approaches.quote: Another time evolution-based heuristic is quantum imaginary time evolution (QITE) [145, 218]... However, QITE is a non-unitary evolution and can be challenging to implement on a quantum computer [145]. Thus, only heuristic approximations of QITE exist to the best of our knowledge. These include projecting the non-unitary evolution to unitary operations [145] or embedding it in a unitary of augmented dimension [220]. Another family of algorithms are VQAs that map the time evolution to an ansatz by means of variational principles [218, 221] or directly projecting a Taylor-expansion of the time-evolution operator onto the ansatz [222, 223].
solution_approaches.location: Page 17, Section IV.A.1 Unconstrained Discrete Optimization

solution_approaches.approach: Variational real-time evolution approximating QAA
solution_approaches.description: Variational algorithms for real-time evolution used as heuristics to approximate adiabatic algorithms.
solution_approaches.quote: In addition to variational approximations to QITE, there are also variational approximations to real-time evolution [221, 226]. Those can be used to approximate QAA and form another family of heuristics.
solution_approaches.location: Page 17, Section IV.A.1 Unconstrained Discrete Optimization

solution_approaches.approach: Alternative cost functions (CVaR, Gibbs objective) in VQAs
solution_approaches.description: Use of risk-sensitive or Gibbs-weighted objectives instead of plain expectations to focus on good samples and improve robustness.
solution_approaches.quote: A frequently used example is the Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR) [229, 230], where we do not average over the objective values corresponding to all samples obtained from measuring a quantum state. Instead, we sort them and only take the average over the bestα-fraction of samples... Another proposal is the Gibbs objective function [162]. The rationale is the same as for the CVaR, it puts more emphasize on good samples than on bad samples, i.e., it biases the expectation value.
solution_approaches.location: Page 17-18, Section IV.A.1 Unconstrained Discrete Optimization

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum dynamic programming (quantum DP algorithms)
solution_approaches.description: Exploration of quantum algorithms for dynamic programming, including quantum approximations and heuristics like reinforcement learning.
solution_approaches.quote:
In addition to provable al-
gorithms, can we find good quantum approximations or
heuristics, such as reinforcement learning? Answering
any of these questions will help to further understand
the potential and practical applicability of quantum DP
algorithms and some of them will also be discussed in the
following Sec. IVE.

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum optimization approaches for optimal control / HJB-related problems
solution_approaches.description: Use of quantum optimization methods to find global solutions to contextual bandits, MDPs, and differential-equation-constrained optimization, thereby solving associated HJB equations.
solution_approaches.quote:
In what follows we discuss po-
tential quantum optimization approaches to find global
solutions to the three aforementioned problems:
1. Contextual multi-armed bandit problems.
2. Markov decision processes (MDPs).
3. Optimization problems constrained by differential
equations.

solution_approaches.approach: Value iteration and policy iteration with quantum convex optimization and quadratic speedup
solution_approaches.description: Applying quantum convex optimization (and quadratic speedups from other sections) to value and policy iteration for solving MDPs and related problems.
solution_approaches.quote:
Potential algorithms include:
1. Value iteration and policy iteration boil down to
optimization problems, wherein the convex opti-
mization of Sec. IVB1 could be applicable, perhaps
combinedwiththequadraticspeedupofapproaches
of Sec. IVD.

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum-accelerated reinforcement learning (including LSTD-based methods)
solution_approaches.description: Use of quantum convex optimization and tabular methods to accelerate reinforcement learning algorithms such as LSTD and approximate value/policy iteration.
solution_approaches.quote:
2. Reinforcement learning is a broad family of ap-
proaches, rather than a single algorithm, which
approximate value or policy iteration, for instance
using Least-Squares Temporal-Difference (LSTD).
Again, the convex optimization of Sec. IVB1 could
be applicable, perhaps together with the tabular
method of Sec. IVD providing additional speedup.

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum reinforcement learning (unitary oracle setting)
solution_approaches.description: Quantum RL algorithms with coherent access to the environment, achieving quadratic speedups for tasks like multi-armed bandits and optimal q-function computation.
solution_approaches.quote:
3. Quantum reinforcement learning (heuristics). In
the unitary oracle setting, from the perspective of
exact methods, that is, algorithms that are guaran-
teed to identify optimal policies in arbitrary envi-
ronment, tight quantum upper and lower bounds
have been identified. In Refs. [325, 326], lower
bounds on the more special task of Multi-arm ban-
dit problems were found, along with essentially
matching quantum upper bounds, for a number of
RL-related tasks, including finding the optimal q-
function. These works achieve a quadratic speedup
over best possible classical methods, assuming ap-
propriate oracle access to the task environment.

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum policy optimization / policy gradient speedups
solution_approaches.description: Quadratic quantum speedups in policy optimization for parameterized policies, including those defined by parameterized quantum circuits.
solution_approaches.quote:
In Jerbiet al.[329] it was shown that quadratic speedups
in policy optimization were possible as long as the poli-
cies satisfy certain regularity conditions, which are, e.g.,
satisfied for policies defined by parameterized quantum
circuits.

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum RL with classical environment access
solution_approaches.description: Quantum enhancements in reinforcement learning when interaction with the environment is classical, yielding super-polynomial advantages under complexity assumptions.
solution_approaches.quote:
However, the second research line investigates quan-
tum enhancements in reinforcement learning when the
access to the task environment is restricted to be clas-
sical. Here too speedups are provably possible, at least
in special cases, but now subject to standard complex-
ity assumptions. For example in Refs. [332, 333] it
was proven that there exist task environments with a
super-polynomial advantage for quantum RL algorithms
(with respect to finding optimal policies and optimal q-
functions), unless the discrete logarithm problem has an
efficient classical solution.

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum stopping time algorithm using Quantum Amplitude Estimation (QAE)
solution_approaches.description: A quantum algorithm leveraging QAE and quantum access to a sampler of the stochastic process to price American options with polynomial speedup.
solution_approaches.quote:
Given quantum ac-
cess to a sampler for the stochastic process, a quantum
algorithm with a polynomial speedup using Quantum
Amplitude Estimation (QAE) [153, 341] was shown by
Doriguello et al.[342].

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum robust optimization via meta algorithms with quantum sampling
solution_approaches.description: Quantum version of robust optimization meta algorithms using quantum access to functions, stochastic gradients, and quantum sampling subroutines with polynomial advantage.
solution_approaches.quote:
Ben-Talet al.[351] devel-
oped meta algorithms to approximately solve the robust
version of a given optimization problem using an oracle
for the solving of the original optimization problem. A
quantum version was developed by Limet al. [352], us-
ing quantum access to the functions, extending the origi-
nal algorithm to include a stochastic gradient, and using

theorem, perhaps most notably the recently proved No

oping new error mitigation methods to produce error-

key_claims.claim: Quantum Monte Carlo integration and gradient estimation can provide a quadratic speedup over classical methods but require significant resource reductions for practical advantage.
key_claims.quote: Quantum Monte Carlo integration and gradient estimation can provide quadratic speedup over classical methods, but more work is required to reduce the amount of quantum resources for early fault-tolerant feasibility and achieving an actual speedup.

key_claims.claim: Quantum algorithms for stochastic modeling, optimization, and machine learning are broadly applicable to financial problems.
key_claims.quote: Quantum algorithms for stochastic modeling, optimization, and machine learning are applicable to a variety of ﬁnancial problems.

key_claims.claim: Current quantum hardware is in a nascent NISQ stage with low fidelity and few qubits, severely limiting solvable problem sizes.
key_claims.quote: Moreover, current quantum hardware is still in a nascent stage, existing noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices (NISQ) have low ﬁdelity and a small number of qubits, which severely limits the size of problems that can be solved.

key_claims.claim: End-to-end quantum advantage in commercially relevant financial problems is challenged by data loading, readout, and pre/post-processing costs.
key_claims.quote: In particular, a large amount of work needs to be done to reduce the resource requirements in certain components of the algorithms, such as quantum embedding of classical input data, readout of the quantum output, and pre- and post-processing. Otherwise, the complexity of these components may signiﬁcantly disparage the speedup obtained from other components of the algorithm.

key_claims.claim: The overhead from current quantum error correcting codes could prevent the quadratic speedup of QMCI from being realizable in practice.
key_claims.quote: In addition, it has been noted that the overhead from current quantum error correcting codes could prevent the quadratic speedup from being realizable 28.
key_claims.location: Page 3, Quantum methods for Monte Carlo-based pricing and risk analysis, paragraph 2

key_claims.claim: State preparation for QMCI is a major bottleneck, especially for concentrated distributions and tabulated data.
key_claims.quote:
Despite the general applicability of these algorithms, their inverse dependence on the ﬁlling ratio (the relevant norm of the function divided by the corresponding norm of the bounding box of that function) of the function being loaded, makes these algorithms much less efﬁcient when the target distribution is concentrated around a few values.
...
For loading tabulated data, one has to resort to generic data loading techniques 47–49, which in general scale linearly with the number of data points to be loaded.
key_claims.location: Page 4, Quantum methods for Monte Carlo-based pricing and risk analysis, paragraph on state preparation

key_claims.claim: It remains an open question whether there are unitary procedures for loading payoff distributions that avoid heavy arithmetic and scale sublinearly in qubits.
key_claims.quote: Therefore, it remains an open question whether there are alternative unitary procedures for loading the payoff distribution that avoid signiﬁcant arithmetic and have sublinear scaling in the number of qubits.
key_claims.location: Page 4, Quantum methods for Monte Carlo-based pricing and risk analysis, paragraph on joint distribution loading

key_claims.claim: For PDE-based pricing, quantum linear systems algorithms can offer exponential reduction in dimension dependence but suffer from sampling overhead similar to QMCI.
key_claims.quote: Whereas under various assumptions about the conditioning of the linear systems and data-access model, the quantum linear system can be solved with an exponential reduction in the dependence on the dimension, a sampling cost needs to be paid to readout the solution from the quantum state, making this technique reminiscent of classical and quantum MCI.
key_claims.location: Page 5, Quantum methods for differential-equation-based pricing and risk analysis, paragraph 2

key_claims.claim: For structured convex programs like SCPs, there is currently only a small margin for practical quantum speedup because classical methods are already very efficient.
key_claims.quote: Considering that SCPs can be solved very efﬁciently classically, there is a small margin for quantum speedup in practice.
key_claims.location: Page 6, Quantum methods for continuous optimization, paragraph 4

key_claims.claim: Quantum BLAS-based speedups are challenged by conditioning dependence, sampling costs, and data loading requirements.
key_claims.quote: However, a quantum BLAS (QBLAS) 59, 87 comes with three notable caveats that make it challenging to compare quantum and classical worst-case complexities. First, a QBLAS operates on the spectrum of matrices and thus has polynomial dependence on the conditioning of the matrix, which classically typically appears only in iterative algorithms. Second, retrieving data from a quantum device requires sampling and consequently incurs a classical sampling cost that depends poorly on the desired error. Lastly, the algorithms require access to the classical data in quantum superposition, which can only be done efﬁciently without quantum memory in certain cases when the input matrices are sparse.
key_claims.location: Page 6–7, Quantum methods for continuous optimization, paragraph on QBLAS caveats

key_claims.claim: It is still an open question whether quantum computation can provide an advantage for structured convex programs in general, including finance.
key_claims.quote: Currently, it seems to still be an open question whether quantum computation can provide an advantage for structured convex programs in general, and not just ﬁnance.
key_claims.location: Page 7–8, Quantum methods for continuous optimization, paragraph on overall assessment

key_claims.claim: Quantum walk search can provide almost quadratic speedup for tree search, but integration of practical heuristics and overall time-to-solution advantages remain unclear.
key_claims.quote: Ref. 120 developed quantum-walk-search-based techniques, which provide an almost quadratic speedup for tree search in terms of the size of the tree. However, this does not allow the integration of search heuristics or early stopping, both of which have been found to signiﬁcantly boost the performance of classical algorithms on typical problem instances.
key_claims.location: Page 8, Quantum methods for discrete optimization, paragraph on QWS

key_claims.claim: For quantum simulated annealing, it is unclear whether all parameter dependencies can be improved over classical MCMC, and classical SA is usually used heuristically.
key_claims.quote: However, it’s still unclear whether, in general, the dependence on all parameters with quantum can be made better than or even match the dependence they have with classical MCMC 128. Furthermore, classical SA is typically used as a heuristic and not run until the Markov chains have converged to their stationary distributions129, 130.
key_claims.location: Page 8–9, Quantum methods for discrete optimization, paragraph on SA

key_claims.claim: Variational quantum algorithms face challenges such as NP-hard parameter tuning and barren plateaus, though convergence can occur in over-parameterized regimes.
key_claims.quote: Variational quantum algorithms usually suffer from difﬁculties in tuning the variational parameters and hyperparameters, which by itself can be NP-hard157. In addition, for certain initializations, the gradients with respect to the parameters can vanish even when the model is far from convergence158, 159, requiring exponentially-many samples to estimate them. Still, the convergence of VQE has been demonstrated in the over-parameterized regime 160, even with exponentially-small gradients.
key_claims.location: Page 9, Quantum methods for discrete optimization, paragraph on variational algorithms

key_claims.claim: Quantum ML algorithms that accelerate classical techniques typically require error-corrected quantum computers and quantum memory, whose feasibility is unclear.
key_claims.quote:
Quantum algorithms for ML can be further divided into method s for accelerating classical techniques, typically by
applying QBLASs, and quantum-native algorithms, which att empt to harness the classical intractability of quantum
simulation to build more expressive models. The former typi cally requires an error-corrected quantum computer,
whereas, it is argued that, the later may not and is more near t erm42. ... The most notable
one being data loading, and unfortunately, most of these alg orithms work in a setting with quantum memory 179, 180.
It is currently unclear if such a device can be constructed.

key_claims.claim: Many QBLAS-based quantum ML algorithms only yield speedups for low-rank data and not exponential speedups as once thought.
key_claims.quote:
F urthermore, a variety of these approaches only provide
speedups when the data has low-rank approximations, and in t his setting, the speedup is not exponential as it was once
thought.

key_claims.claim: It is unclear whether quantum-native models provide advantage on classical (non-quantum-generated) problems.
key_claims.quote:
Quantum-native models, such as quantum neural networks, qu antum circuit Born machine and quantum kernel
methods, circumvent the issues of QBLASs and can be intracta ble to classically simulate, however, it is currently
unclear if they provide advantage on classical problems.

key_claims.claim: Initial numerical evidence suggests the expressivity advantage of quantum-native models does not extend to classical problems.
key_claims.quote:
Sp eciﬁcally, although these methods can be more expressive,
this has only been shown to provide advantage for problems in volving data generated from quantum processes 182.
In addition, initial numerical evidence suggests this does not extend to classical problems 183.

key_claims.claim: Parameterized quantum methods like QNNs are challenging to train and lack efficient backpropagation comparable to classical NNs.
key_claims.quote:
Parameterized quan-
tum methods, such as QNNs, can be challenging to train in gene ral158 and do not currently have back-propagation
algorithms that are as efﬁcient as those for classical NNs.

key_claims.claim: Further research is needed to determine if exponential speedup of classical ML problems is still possible with quantum computing.
key_claims.quote:
However, there remain some quantum ML algorithms t hat do not rely on this low-rank assumption and may
remain impervious to dequantization 181. Further research is needed to determine if an exponential s peedup of classical
ML problems is still possible with quantum computing.

key_claims.claim: Quantum circuit learning with low-depth circuits implies important application opportunities in quantum algorithms for finance.
key_claims.quote:
This technique
is dubbed as quantum circuit learning 192, and has been numerically shown to allow for a low-depth circ uit, hence
implying important application opportunities in quantum a lgorithms for ﬁnance.

key_claims.claim: Quantum boosting algorithms reduce dependence on VC dimension but require access to quantum examples, which is a major limitation.
key_claims.quote:
Ref. 208 demonstrated a quantization of the
AdaBoost algorithm, which promises a quadratic reduction i n the dependence on the VC dimension. ... A major limitation for both approaches is that they need to h ave access to quantum examples,
which requires preparing quantum states encoding distribu tions over the training data.

key_claims.claim: Generative quantum ML leveraging sampling advantages is particularly promising for finance because many applications require sampling from complex distributions.
key_claims.quote:
One of the most promising
aspects of achieving potential quantum advantage lies in th e sampling advantage of quantum computers, especially
considering that many applications in ﬁnance require gener ating samples from complex distributions.

key_claims.claim: QCBM at least matches and can surpass restricted Boltzmann machines as model size scales.

key_claims.location: Page 12 – Quantum methods for generative learning

key_claims.claim: QGANs may exhibit exponential advantage over classical adversarial networks when data are measurements from high-dimensional spaces.
key_claims.quote:
The authors showed that when the da ta consists of samples of measurements made on high-
dimensional spaces, quantum adversarial networks may exhi bit an exponential advantage over classical adversarial
networks.
key_claims.location: Page 12 – Quantum methods for generative learning

key_claims.claim: Quantum-inspired dequantized algorithms refute many originally claimed exponential quantum speedups for ML but may still inspire useful algorithms for high-dimensional financial problems.
key_claims.quote:
Despite these algorithms refuting much of the originally c laimed exponential quantum speedups for ML,
they could potentially inspire useful algorithms for high- dimensional ﬁnancial problems.

key_claims.claim: It is still unclear whether proposed quantum approaches for stochastic modeling, optimization and ML can yield end-to-end quantum advantage on practical financial problems.
key_claims.quote:
Promising provable quantum advantages
have been discovered in certain black-box settings, such as MCI. However, it is still unclear whether any of these pro-
posed approaches for stochastic modeling, optimization an d ML can be turned into an end-to-end quantum advantage
on practical problems.

key_claims.claim: The financial industry is well positioned to be an early adopter of quantum computing because computational time and accuracy directly impact profit and loss.
key_claims.quote:
In ﬁnance, computational time and ac curacy can often directly translate to the proﬁt and loss
of the business for which the problems are being solved, inso much that any actual wall-clock speedup and associated
model performance improvement that new forms of computing c ould bring can have a tremendous impact on the ﬁnan-
cial industry. ... As a result , the ﬁnancial industry is perfectly positioned to be an earl y
adopter and take full advantage of quantum computing in the ﬁ eld of computational ﬁnance.

key_claims.claim: State preparation, especially loading classical probability distributions, is a common bottleneck in quantum algorithms for stochastic modeling in finance.
key_claims.quote:
As mentione d earlier, state preparation, speciﬁcally the loading of
quantum states encoding classical probability distributi ons, is a common task required in quantum algorithms for
stochastic modeling.

key_claims.claim: Financial problems are typically highly constrained, so native multi-qubit and specialized two-qubit interactions could significantly reduce circuit complexity for QAOA and quantum ML.
key_claims.quote:
As mentioned in the Optimization section, ﬁnancial proble ms
are typically highly constrained. Moreover, having access to a variety of native entangling gates may also motivate the
design and implementation of more efﬁcient circuits for qua ntum ML182.

key_claims.claim: Existing quantum memory technologies have fundamental limitations that make scalable, low-cost quantum memory without active error correction highly challenging.
key_claims.quote:
However, it has been recently highlighted that existing qu antum memory technologies have
fundamental limitations that make the realization of low-c ost and scalable quantum memory without active error cor-
rection highly challenging 290.

key_claims.claim: Current quantum hardware has much slower operation clock rates than classical computers, limiting practical usability of many quantum algorithms, especially variational ML.
key_claims.quote:
Additionally, the operation clock rate of the current quant um hardware is much slower compared to classical
computers; this is also a limiting factor in the practical us ability of many quantum algorithms. For example, quantum
variational algorithms for ML require a large number of high -quality circuit evaluations to estimate gradients throug h
sampling.

key_claims.claim: Current quantum error correction introduces significant overhead that may negate certain quantum speedups for finance.
key_claims.quote:
Moreover, current quantum error correction techniques
introduce a signiﬁcant additional overhead that potential ly negates certain quantum speedups for ﬁnance 28.

key_claims.claim: There remain many quantum-algorithmic challenges to achieve real-world quantum advantage in finance, but advancing hardware will enable benchmarking of more complex algorithms.
key_claims.quote:
We hope that this Review has highlighted that in addition to challenges in hardware technologies there are still a lot
of interesting quantum-algorithmic challenges to overcom e to bring about a real-world quantum advantage. As quan-
tum hardware advances, we expect to be able to benchmark more complex quantum algorithms, especially heuristic
ones, on interesting problems.

problem_domains.problem: Complex optimization problems in logistics and finance
problem_domains.description: The paper frames complex optimization problems, including those in finance, as currently intractable or difficult for classical computers and as a key target for quantum computing.
problem_domains.quote: Complex optimization problems, such as those encountered in logistics and finance, can be addressed using quantum computers as well.

problem_domains.description: Risk analysis and portfolio optimization are described as complex financial tasks involving large data and predictions about asset performance.
problem_domains.quote: Quantum computers could be used to perform risk analysis and optimize portfolios. In the field of finance, quantum computers have the potential to revolutionize risk analysis and portfolio optimization. These are complex tasks that involve analysing large amounts of data and making predictions about the performance of financial assets.

problem_domains.description: The document focuses on benchmarking quantum and classical methods for solving optimization problems.
problem_domains.quote: In the following section, we focus on benchmarking goals related to understanding the potential of quantum computers for solving optimization problems in terms of a fair comparison.

problem_domains.problem: comparison of classical and quantum algorithms
problem_domains.description: The need to compare classical and quantum optimization algorithms to demonstrate quantum advantage.
problem_domains.quote: One of the main goals of benchmarking in the present context is the comparison of classical and quantum algorithms — aiming at demonstrating quantum advantage.

problem_domains.problem: tracking progress in hardware and algorithmic developments
problem_domains.description: Using benchmarks to monitor improvements in quantum hardware and optimization algorithms over time.
problem_domains.quote: Benchmarking may also be executed to track the progress in hardware developments (cf. Sec. VIA) as well as algorithmic improvements.

problem_domains.description: Determining how optimization algorithms scale with problem size and when they fail to provide good solutions.
problem_domains.quote: Furthermore, benchmarking can give us insights into an algorithm’s scaling behavior: Is there a problem scale at which algorithms fail to provide good solutions — possibly due to hardware limitations?

problem_domains.description: Deciding whether benchmarks should be defined on the original optimization problem or on a specific mathematical model.
problem_domains.quote: For benchmarks, it is therefore crucial to decide on the level a problem is defined: either model-independent, i.e., on the level of the original optimization problem, which allows different mathematical modeling methods, or model-dependent, i.e., on the level of a concrete mathematical model.

problem_domains.description: Using pre-processing to reduce problem size and complexity before applying optimization algorithms.
problem_domains.quote: The goal of pre-processing is to modify the problem in such a way that it allows the optimization algorithm to work more efficiently.

problem_domains.description: Choosing the best-suited hardware platform (classical or quantum, analog or digital) for a given optimization problem.
problem_domains.quote: Tailoring the choice of platform to the characteristics of the problem at hand – if possible – can lead to better outcomes. This approach aligns with the idea of platform-aware optimization, ensuring that the selected platform is optimally matched to the unique requirements of the problem being addressed.

problem_domains.description: Designing benchmarks that allow fair comparison between very different classical and quantum systems.
problem_domains.quote: To understand the advantages and disadvantages of different platforms for different optimization problems, performing cross-platform benchmarking is crucial. At the same time, such benchmarks pose a particular challenge, as they must allow a fair comparison between systems that can function very differently.

problem_domains.description: Choosing metrics (resource cost, run time, quality, problem complexity) that enable fair comparison of optimization solvers.
problem_domains.quote: Due to the technological differences between classical and quantum systems, the selection of a set of metrics that enable a fair comparison is crucial. The four main metric categories that suffice said criteria are resource cost, run time, quality, and problem complexity.

problem_domains.problem: identifying standardized quantum optimization benchmark problems
problem_domains.description: Finding model-independent problems that are hard for classical solvers but suitable for current and near-term quantum technologies.
problem_domains.quote: Next, we present a set of model-independent problems that show promise for establishing standardized quantum optimization benchmarks. The problems should be chosen sufficiently hard for state-of-the-art classical solvers to leave a margin for quantum methods but within an intermediate size range where current and/or near-term quantum technologies can be effectively deployed.

problem_domains.description: Stochastic optimization of an energy retailer’s advance purchases and storage usage to minimize total energy procurement cost under uncertain demand, storage levels, and spot prices.
problem_domains.quote: Use case 3: Energy retailing with storage. Consider an energy retailer that delivers energy to end customers. The energy supplier buys energy from energy producers in advance, e.g., on the day-ahead energy trading market, in one-hour time intervals, where the electricity price depends on several factors such as energy demand, renewable energy generation, etc. Additionally, the energy supplier has access to an energy storage system, e.g., a fleet of EVs that act as a virtual power plant, that can accumulate energy when this is cheap, to later use it when energy demand is high. The energy supplier’s goal is to deliver energy to its customers at the lowest possible cost.

problem_domains.problem: Stochastic unconstrained optimization of energy procurement
problem_domains.description: Formulation of the retailer’s decision on how much cheap energy to buy each hour to minimize expected total cost including expensive balancing energy, under random demand, storage, and high-price processes.
problem_domains.quote: We can formulate the problem mathematically as follows. Let ek ∈ R≥0 be the decision variable indicating the MWh the energy supplier buys in each hour k ∈ { 0, 1, . . . , K − 1} in advance, usually with K = 24, and p_k^low ∈ R the price of the cheap energy (which sometimes might even be negative!). Similarly, let Dk, Bk, Pk^high be random variables that capture, respectively, the electricity demand at time k in MWh, the energy available in storage at time k in MWh, and the price of the expensive energy at time k. The optimization problem is the following: ... That is, we have a stochastic unconstrained optimization where the objective function at time k consists of two terms: the cost of buying cheap energy, and the expected cost of buying expensive energy.
problem_domains.location: Page 50, section 'VII ILLUSTRATIVE APPLICATIONS', 'Use case 3: Energy retailing with storage'

problem_domains.problem: Convex energy procurement optimization (baseline, not quantum-challenging)

problem_domains.quote: The optimization in Eq. (36) is convex since the objective function is piece-wise linear and convex. Thus, if Dk, Bk, and Pk^high are random variables independent of the decision variables, we can efficiently solve the problem with conventional convex optimization tools, in fact, by solving K separate problems — one for every term in the sum in Eq. (36). Hence, Eq. (36), in its current form, is not a promising problem candidate for demonstrating quantum advantage.
problem_domains.location: Page 50, section 'VII ILLUSTRATIVE APPLICATIONS', 'Use case 3: Energy retailing with storage'

problem_domains.problem: Energy retailing with storage and decision-dependent dynamics (optimal control formulation)
problem_domains.description: More realistic version where storage levels depend on past charging/discharging decisions, coupling time steps and turning the problem into an optimal control problem.
problem_domains.quote: 1. The energy available in storage at time k depends on the previous decisions taken; for example, on how EVs charge and discharge, as in the previous use case 2. ... In particular, (1) couples the random variables with the decision variables and “links” the K timesteps, i.e., terms in the objective function Eq. (36). This is similar to the system dynamics function in optimal control, cf. Sec. IVE. ... We can recast Eq. (36) as an optimal control problem where the system dynamics are given by the algorithm in the second use case, i.e., the energy available by how EVs charge and discharge.
problem_domains.location: Page 50, section 'VII ILLUSTRATIVE APPLICATIONS', 'Use case 3: Energy retailing with storage'

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum optimization
solution_approaches.description: The general use of quantum algorithms to improve optimization performance across solution quality, diversity, time, and cost.

Quantum computing could revolutionize numerous do-
mains in business and science, with optimization fre-
quently identified as a prime candidate to profit from

Techniques like Grover’s search [1], quantum

algorithms will not necessarily improve the performance

solution_approaches.approach: Grover Search for constrained discrete optimization

solution_approaches.approach: quantum branch and bound algorithm
solution_approaches.description: Adapts Grover Search to branch-and-bound trees to accelerate classical branch-and-bound algorithms.
solution_approaches.quote: In [254], a quantum branch and bound algorithm is introduced that accelerates classical branch-and-bound algorithms. It is shown that it solves most instances of the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model to optimality with a high probability in time O(20.226n). The algorithm adapts Grover Search to be applicable to search branch-and-bound trees.
solution_approaches.location: Page 18, Section IV PROBLEM CLASSES & ALGORITHMS

solution_approaches.approach: constraint-preserving ansatz in VQAs (Dicke state, particle-preserving ansatz)
solution_approaches.description: Designs ansätze restricted to the feasible subspace, e.g., fixed Hamming weight via Dicke states or particle-preserving gates.
solution_approaches.quote: The most straight-forward approach is to design an ansatz that – in the noise-free case – is restricted to the feasible space. For instance, suppose a constraint that fixes the Hamming weight of feasible bit strings, i.e., the number of ones. Then, we can prepare as initial state a uniform superposition of all these feasible bit strings, i.e., a Dicke state [255]. Or, we can use a parametric iSWAP or a Givens rotation gate, like in a particle preserving ansatz in quantum chemistry [256], to construct an ansatz that only generates feasible bit strings.
solution_approaches.location: Page 18, Section IV PROBLEM CLASSES & ALGORITHMS

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum Alternating Operator Ansatz (QAOA’)
solution_approaches.description: Generalizes QAOA with mixers and initial states tailored to hard constraints, keeping objective structure and cheaper cost operators.
solution_approaches.quote: The Quantum Alternating Operator Ansatz (QAOA’) [257, 258] generalizes the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm to much wider classes of problems and encodings, in particular to problems with hard constraints.
solution_approaches.location: Page 18, Section IV PROBLEM CLASSES & ALGORITHMS

solution_approaches.quote: The first quantum algorithms for SDPs were first order methods, based on the Multiplicative Weights Update (MWU) framework [272]. In this framework one uses candidate solutions X that are proportional to ρ = exp(∑m i=1 yiAi)/ tr(exp(∑m i=1 yiAi)) for some (sparse) vector y ∈ Rm.

solution_approaches.approach: quantum IPMs using quantum linear system solvers and tomography
solution_approaches.description: Accelerates Newton steps in interior point methods via quantum linear system algorithms followed by state tomography.

solution_approaches.quote: Very recently, a quantum speedup for interior point methods was achieved without introducing a dependence on a condition number [291]. Under some mild assumptions and access to QRAM, this IPM achieves a quantum speedup for linear programs in which the number of linear inequalities m is much larger than the number of variables n

solution_approaches.approach: quantum SDP-solvers for MAXCUT via Gibbs state preparation
solution_approaches.description: Reduces MAXCUT SDP feasibility to preparing a Gibbs state with specific properties and uses MWU with specialized oracles.
solution_approaches.quote: Brandao et al. [181] demonstrated that, after normalizing the diagonal constraints by n and relaxing slightly the constraints, feasibility reduces the task of solving the MAXCUT SDP to a possibly simpler task: preparing a Gibbs state that is (i) approximately indistinguishable from the maximally mixed state when measured in the computational basis, and (ii) whose trace inner product with C is close to an estimate of the optimal objective value, determined via binary search.
solution_approaches.location: Page 20, Section IV.B.1 Quantum SDP-solvers for approximating MAXCUT

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum Hamiltonian Descent (QHD)

tential quantum optimization approaches to find global

3. Quantum reinforcement learning (heuristics). In

ing algorithms (with respect to finding optimal policies

ers [197, 198]. In addition, the QAOA mixer can be
changed to include constraints of the optimization prob-
lem[258,397], e.g., for equality constraints[259,260]. Al-

where m > n . ... As discussed in Sec. IVA1, this allows

solution_approaches.approach: Transpilation optimizations including SWAP networks and structure-aware routing
