solution_approaches.quote:
For example, QAOA results in
circuits with blocks of commuting two-qubit gates. Ex-
ploiting this structure results in shallower quantum cir-
cuits [402, 418, 429–431]. More precisely, if the topol-
ogy of the problem graph does not perfectly match the
coupling map of the QPU, SWAP gates are necessary
to enable two qubit gates between unconnected qubits.
The denser the graph, the more SWAP gates are neces-
sary which results in a deeper circuit [402].

solution_approaches.approach: Dynamic circuits to address limited connectivity

solution_approaches.quote:

such as dynamic circuits [432]. In a dynamic circuit some
of the qubits are measured and the outcome of these
measurements changes the following circuit instructions
within the coherence time of the qubits. For instance,
this offers additional possibilities to address limited qubit
connectivity [433]. As an example, the SWAP based im-
plementation of the QAOA problem graph may be re-
placed on grid-like QPU coupling maps by constant depth
circuits with a quadratic auxiliary qubit overhead [434].

prompted the development of PEA [16], a probabilistic

zero-noise limit.

methods reduce the noise in quantum circuits without

key_claims.claim: Quantum optimization improvements could occur across solution quality, diversity, time-to-solution, and cost-to-solution.
key_claims.quote:
Moreover, these improvements could oc-
cur across multiple dimensions, such as solution quality,
solution diversity, time-to-solution, and cost-to-solution.

key_claims.claim: Quantum optimization algorithms can complement classical algorithms and synergies between them can lead to better performance.
key_claims.quote:
Quantum optimization algorithms pro-
vide additional tools that complement existing ones, and
synergies with classical algorithms can certainly lead to
better performance.
key_claims.location: Section II. QUANTUM ADVANTAGE & COMPLEXITY THEORY (Page 3, last paragraph before Section II heading)

key_claims.claim: Understanding complexity theory is useful for gauging possible quantum advantage in optimization, but strict complexity-theoretic separations are neither necessary nor sufficient for practical advantage.
key_claims.quote:
The main
takeaway for this section can be summarized as follows:
Understanding complexity theory is extremely useful for
gauging possible quantum advantage in optimization,
but rigorous complexity-theoretic separations are not
necessary, nor sufficient when seeking a practical
quantum advantage.
key_claims.location: Section II. QUANTUM ADVANTAGE & COMPLEXITY THEORY (Page 3)

key_claims.claim: It is unlikely that quantum computers provide exponential speedups for NP-hard problems, but exponential speedups for NP-intermediate problems cannot be ruled out.
key_claims.quote:
It is unlikely, that quantum computers provide expo-
nential speedups for NP-hard (and thus, NPO-hard)
problems. See [40] for stronger hypotheses along these
lines. But exponential speedups for an interesting sub-
class of NP problems, not complete but also not inP,
called NP-intermediate, cannot be ruled out.
key_claims.location: Section II.A.3. Hard versus complete problems (Page 5–6)

key_claims.claim: Most complexity-theoretic statements deal with worst-case instances, whereas practical optimization often concerns typical instances where quantum speedups may still be possible.
key_claims.quote:
It is important to emphasize the following point:
Complexity theory is traditionally focused on worst-case
problem instances. In practice, one often needs to solve
a “typical” instance which may be much easier than the
hardest, worst-case instance.
key_claims.location: Section II.A.5. Worst-case complexity and fixed-parameter tractability (Page 6)

key_claims.claim: Quantum algorithms might provide speedups even if they only match classical approximation ratios, by improving computational efficiency.
key_claims.quote:
Further, quantum optimization methods might provide
provable and computational speedups, even if they sim-
ply match the approximation factors of classical algo-
rithms.

key_claims.claim: Quantum heuristic methods are motivated by the success of classical heuristics and aim to provide reasonable solutions where classical approaches are too slow or ineffective.
key_claims.quote:
The success of classical
heuristic algorithms indeed motivates the study of quan-
tum heuristic methods, where the aim of the latter is to
design algorithms that leverage quantum computation to
provide reasonable solutions to problems where classical
approaches either cannot, or simply take too long to do
so.
key_claims.location: Section II.C. Heuristics in Quantum Optimization (Page 8)

key_claims.claim: Barren plateaus are a central bottleneck for scaling variational quantum algorithms to practically relevant problem sizes.
key_claims.quote:
An important feature in the
study of landscapes are so-calledbarren plateaus[72–79],
especially in conjunction with variational quantum al-
gorithms, which correspond to loss landscapes that are
exponentially flat in the number of system qubits. In
fact, this phenomenon provides a central bottleneck in
the scaling of variational quantum algorithms to practi-
cally relevant problem sizes.
key_claims.location: Section II.C. Heuristics in Quantum Optimization (Page 8)

key_claims.claim: Average-case hard optimization problems with Overlap Gap Property may be hard for classical and low-depth quantum algorithms, but might be addressable by more sophisticated quantum algorithms, offering potential superpolynomial advantage.
key_claims.quote:
Additionally, problems with a so-called
Overlap Gap Property (OGP) [92] have been proven to
be average-case hard for certain families of classical algo-
rithms (and local low-depth quantum algorithms), but it
remainsunclearwhethertheseproblemscanbeaddressed
by higher-depth and/or more sophisticated quantum al-
gorithms [93–96]. If so, this would be very convincing
evidence for useful superpolynomial quantum advantage,
since such problems naturally arise in combinatorial opti-
mization, statistical physics and high-dimensional statis-
tics.
key_claims.location: Section II.D. Takeaways from Complexity Theory in Quantum Optimization (Page 9)

key_claims.claim: Grover-based quantum branch-and-bound can accelerate classical branch-and-bound but requires fault-tolerant quantum computing and loses a posteriori optimality bounds.
key_claims.quote: While this has the potential to accelerate classical schemes, it has the disadvantage that no a posteriori bounds on the optimality gap are generated, which often allow an early termination of such search schemes. Further, it requires FTQC, which adds additional overhead.
key_claims.location: Page 18, Section IV PROBLEM CLASSES & ALGORITHMS

key_claims.claim: Efficient handling of constraints is crucial for achieving quantum advantage in optimization.
key_claims.quote: Since constraints are appearing almost everywhere in practice, further progress on how to efficiently handle them is crucial on the path towards quantum advantage in optimization.
key_claims.location: Page 18, Section IV PROBLEM CLASSES & ALGORITHMS

key_claims.claim: Quantum MWU-based SDP solvers often suffer from poor scaling in the scale-invariant parameter γ = Rr/ϵ, limiting practical speedups.
key_claims.quote: Often, this parameter γ scales poorly in terms of n and m [165], especially when parameters r, R scale linearly or superlinearly with n.

key_claims.claim: QRAM is a critical but currently impractical assumption for many quantum optimization algorithms.
key_claims.quote: Although concrete proposals exist [275, 276], a scalable fault-tolerant implementation is yet to be found [277–280], making this at best a long-term prospect.

key_claims.claim: Quantum IPMs can improve dependence on problem size but may not yield overall speedup due to condition number and precision issues.
key_claims.quote: Overall, assuming access to QRAM, quantum IPMs achieve favorable dependence on the size of the problem (m and n) for linear and semidefinite optimization compared to classical algorithms, but the remaining dependence on some numerical parameters (e.g., a condition number bound for the Newton systems) makes it unclear if an overall speedup is achieved.
key_claims.location: Page 20, Section IV.B.1 Second order methods

key_claims.claim: A provable quantum speedup for certain large LPs via IPM without condition-number dependence has been achieved.
key_claims.quote: Very recently, a quantum speedup for interior point methods was achieved without introducing a dependence on a condition number [291].
key_claims.location: Page 20, Section IV.B.1 Second order methods

key_claims.claim: The initial MAXCUT SDP quantum algorithm has prohibitive precision dependence, but later work achieves polynomial speedup with improved error scaling under QRAM.
key_claims.quote: However, the algorithm exhibits a poor O(ϵ−28) dependence on precision, prohibiting an overall speedup. The impractical error scaling was addressed by Augustino et al.[174], where iterative refinement techniques are used to exponentially improve the dependence on the inverse precision
key_claims.location: Page 20, Section IV.B.1 Quantum SDP-solvers for approximating MAXCUT

key_claims.claim: Quantum matrix scaling algorithms achieve speedups without introducing condition number dependence.
key_claims.quote: Importantly, these quantum algorithms do not introduce a dependence on a condition number.
key_claims.location: Page 20, Section IV.B.1 Quantum algorithms for matrix scaling and matrix balancing

key_claims.claim: In black-box convex and non-convex optimization, quantum algorithms cannot beat classical lower bounds on query complexity in general.
key_claims.quote: Echoing the situation in convex optimization [267], there are clear limits as to the speedup in non-convex optimization [304].

key_claims.claim: Quantum SGD can offer query advantages only in certain dimensional regimes.
key_claims.quote: the algorithm requires O(√nϵ−3) queries, which is only better than the classical algorithm O(ϵ−4) when the dimension is < ϵ −2.

key_claims.claim: Quantum simulated annealing via quantum walks can provide polynomial speedups over classical simulated annealing.
key_claims.quote: Quantum computers obtain polynomial speedups in executing the classical simulated annealing process via quantum walks [308].

key_claims.claim: There is a plausible prospect of super-quadratic quantum speedups for branch-and-bound on NP-hard problems.
key_claims.quote: It seems plausible that it could allow for super-quadratic speedup for NP-hard problems quite generically, a tantalizing prospect.

key_claims.claim: For many DP problems with hypercube structure, quantum algorithms achieve at most quadratic speedup, and for some other structures no speedup is known.
key_claims.quote: One can formulate a generic DP problem with the DP table in the form of hypercube and show that, in the generic case, the quantum speedup can be at most quadratic [338]. It is an open problem whether quantum speedups can be obtained for algorithms with a DP table of a different structure.

key_claims.claim: For edit distance, there is a strong quantum lower bound and no known quantum speedup.
key_claims.quote: Quantumly, no quantum speedup is known but an eΩ(n1.5) quantum lower bound is known for the generic case [40, 344].

key_claims.claim: For MIP, it is unclear what level of quantum subroutine advantage is needed to yield overall optimization speedup.
key_claims.quote: However, it is unclear what advantage the sub-routine needs to provide to imply an overall advantage of the optimization algorithm for MIP.

key_claims.claim: Quantum reinforcement learning with unitary oracular access can achieve quadratic speedups over the best possible classical methods for certain RL tasks including multi-armed bandits.
key_claims.quote:
These works achieve a quadratic speedup
over best possible classical methods, assuming ap-
propriate oracle access to the task environment.
key_claims.location: Page 26-27, Section IV PROBLEM CLASSES & ALGORITHMS

key_claims.claim: Quantum policy optimization with parameterized quantum circuits can achieve quadratic speedups, and these cannot be improved further in general.
key_claims.quote:
In Jerbi et al.[354] it was shown that quadratic speedups
in policy optimization were possible as long as the poli-
cies satisfy certain regularity conditions, which are, e.g.,
satisfied for policies defined by parameterized quantum
circuits. The lower bounds for this problem have been
established for a more general setting by Cornelissen et
al. [355] and they show that these quadratic improve-
ments cannot be improved further.
key_claims.location: Page 27, Section IV PROBLEM CLASSES & ALGORITHMS

key_claims.claim: There exist task environments where quantum reinforcement learning with classical access has superpolynomial advantage under standard complexity assumptions.
key_claims.quote:
For example in Refs. [357, 358] it was
proven that there exist task environments with a super-
polynomial advantage for quantum reinforcement learn-
ing algorithms (with respect to finding optimal policies
and optimal q-functions), unless the discrete logarithm
problem has an efficient classical solution.
key_claims.location: Page 27, Section IV PROBLEM CLASSES & ALGORITHMS

key_claims.claim: Quantum robust optimization meta-algorithms can achieve polynomial advantage using quantum sampling and stochastic gradients.
key_claims.quote:
A
quantum version was developed by Lim et al. [377], us-
ing quantum access to the functions, extending the origi-
nal algorithm to include a stochastic gradient, and using
quantum sampling subroutines with polynomial advan-
tage.

key_claims.claim: Quantum-native algorithms for Multi-Objective Optimization are largely unexplored and represent an interesting domain for future research.
key_claims.quote:
There is only very little literature considering quantum
optimization algorithms for MOO. ... Thus, quantum-
native algorithms for MOO present a very interesting do-
main for future research.

key_claims.claim: Existing quantum RL algorithms with coherent access have significant limitations, including the need for fault tolerance and coherent environment access, and may not yield practical wall-clock speedups on early devices.
key_claims.quote:
We note that the algorithms listed above have signifi-
cant limitations, including the fact that they require fault
tolerance, and that quadratic speedups may not translate
to wall-clock speedups in early fault tolerant quantum
computers. The main conceptual limitation is the re-
quirement to a coherent access to the task environment,
which could only be possible in very restricted or con-
structed cases...
key_claims.location: Page 27, Section IV PROBLEM CLASSES & ALGORITHMS

key_claims.claim: Quantum convex optimization algorithms may be hard to use directly on noisy quantum computers.
key_claims.quote:
In the era of
noisy quantum computers, convex optimization algo-
rithms may be hard to use directly.
key_claims.location: Page 27, Section IV PROBLEM CLASSES & ALGORITHMS (open questions paragraph)

key_claims.claim: Limited qubit connectivity makes dense problem graphs hard to implement efficiently on superconducting devices, favoring sparse instances.
key_claims.quote:
The denser the graph, the more SWAP gates are neces-
sary which results in a deeper circuit [402]. Neverthe-
less, limited qubit connectivity remains an issue and the
problems that scale best on noisy superconducting de-
vices are therefore likely to be those that are not overly
dense [386, 403].

key_claims.claim: Error mitigation methods like PEC and ZNE extend the reach of current devices but can incur large overhead, especially for deep circuits.
key_claims.quote:
Error mitigation techniques use pre- and post-
processing of quantum circuits and measured results to
reduce the impact of hardware noise. While fully elimi-
nating the error comes at an exponential classical over-
head, these methods extend the reach of current devices
even at a limited classical cost [14, 439, 440]. ... PEC is unfeasible in
large scale-experiments since they have a very large γ.
For instance, the γ2 of 60 layers of CNOTs on 127 qubits
was 10128 in Kim et al.[16].
key_claims.location: Page 31, Section V.A.3 Error suppression and mitigation

key_claims.claim: Developing error mitigation methods that produce error-mitigated samples, not just expectation values, is crucial for quantum approximate optimization.
key_claims.quote:
Crucially, to find good solutions, quantum (approximate)
optimization requires sampling from the optimized cir-
cuit. ... Therefore, devel-
oping new error mitigation methods to produce error-
mitigated samples is crucial for the success of quantum
optimization.
key_claims.location: Page 31, Section V.A.3 Error suppression and mitigation

key_claims.claim: General hardware benchmarks like Quantum Volume, EPLG, and CLOPS may fail to predict performance for specific optimization applications, motivating application-tailored benchmarks.
key_claims.quote:
However, these general met-
rics could fail to predict which quantum device will obtain
the best performance, be it in solution quality, execution
speed, or any other criterion, for a specific application.
Therefore, the best possible measure of a quantum com-
puter’s usefulness for optimization is how well it performs
on tasks similar to the problem of interest... We foresee that more application
tailored benchmarks are needed, especially since many
algorithms are heuristic in nature.

key_claims.claim: Theoretical worst-case complexity bounds often fail to describe the difficulty of solving real-world optimization applications, making benchmarking essential.
key_claims.quote:
In fact, theoretical worst case bounds, as
they are discussed in Sec. II, often fail to describe the dif-
ficulties of solving real-world applications that focus on
a specific problem instance of practical use, nor do they
faithfully describe how well practically relevant problems
can be solved for fixed size and data. In this case, we
need to rely on meaningful and systematic benchmarking
of optimization algorithms...

key_claims.claim: Model-independent benchmarks are better suited for long-term comparison across evolving quantum hardware generations.
key_claims.quote: To enable comparability and compatibility for different generations of hardware, model-independent benchmarks are better suited, since they may allow one to leverage new features that might not have been available in earlier generations, such as dynamic quantum circuits [433].

key_claims.claim: Pre-processing can drastically reduce optimization problem size, sometimes removing up to 95% of variables.
key_claims.quote: In fact, it is not uncommon for many problems such as Euclidean TSP or Steiner tree problems in graphs that pre-processing is able to remove 95% of the variables and, hence, reduce the problem size as well as resource requirements significantly [487, 488].

key_claims.claim: Quantum annealing hardware currently suffers from short coherence times and strong environmental coupling, requiring further improvements.
key_claims.quote: The coherence time of current publicly available annealing machines is shorter than the annealing time [506]. This means that these platforms do not achieve closed system dynamics but exhibit strong coupling with the environment. Further hardware improvements are therefore required [507].

key_claims.claim: There is potential for better-performing quantum heuristics, but this requires careful and fair systematic benchmarking.
key_claims.quote: Nevertheless, there is a potential for better performing quantum heuristics, and to show this, we require careful and fair systematic benchmarking.

key_claims.claim: Spin glass problems are average-case hard for many classical algorithms, leaving open the possibility of superpolynomial quantum speedups.
key_claims.quote: Moreover, spin glass problems have properties that make them provably average-case hard for various families of classical algorithms [95]. It remains open as to whether quantum algorithms can do better in these average-case settings, and thus, superpolynomial speedups for spin glass problems are still possible.

key_claims.claim: Certain benchmark problems like MIS, multi-dimensional knapsack, QAP, and sports timetabling remain hard for classical solvers even at modest sizes, making them promising for quantum advantage studies.
key_claims.quote: Still, there exist instances with less than n = 100 variables and m = 8 constraints which cannot be solved to proven optimality. ... It is still considered a computationally nontrivial task to solve to optimality even for modestly sized problems, i.e., n ≈ 30. ... for several medium sized instances no known (and investigated) method was able to find even a single feasible solution [536, 538].

key_claims.claim: Most large-qubit QAOA/VQE experiments use low-density problems due to hardware connectivity and noise limitations.
key_claims.quote: The table illustrates that most experiments with higher qubit numbers have lower problem densities. Increasing the density for a larger number of qubits would require additional SWAP gates, cf. Sec. V, hence, resulting in increased hardware noise.

key_claims.claim: Identifying optimization problems that are promising candidates for practically relevant quantum advantage is challenging due to open questions about algorithm performance and heuristic nature.
key_claims.quote: Identifying optimization problems that are promising candidates for a practically relevant quantum advantage is challenging. This is due to the many open questions about future performance of quantum optimization algo- rithms, as well as the heuristic nature of many of them.

key_claims.claim: Most existing quantum optimization work in finance focuses on small QUBO-based linear and quadratic problems with fewer than 50 variables.
key_claims.quote: The majority of existing quantum optimization re- search in finance focuses on investigating quantum vari- ants of linear and quadratic optimization problems and simplified (mixed) integer programs. Most publications employ a QUBO formulation, combined with a ground state solver such as QAOA or VQE (see Sec. IVA) that is executed on numerical simulators, gate-based hardware, or annealers, typically for systems with less than50 vari- ables.

key_claims.claim: Many classical financial models suffer from approximations and trade-offs due to data issues and the need to balance complexity, computation, and regulation.
key_claims.quote: Despite a century of progress, many models in regu- lated financial institutions suffer from different degrees of approximations and model trade-offs due to irregular and/or scarce information and the need to balance model complexity, computational feasibility, and regulatory, as well as business constraints.

key_claims.claim: Even small improvements in financial optimization can have significant impact, motivating exploration of quantum approaches despite unclear advantage.
key_claims.quote: In many finance problems, even small improvements can have a significant impact. Although, it is still unclear if and how a potential quantum advantage could be real- ized for financial optimization problems – even as the un- derlying technology advances – a thorough understand- ing of the broad spectrum of classical models and their limitations in the financial industry could help guide the development of quantum optimization approaches...

key_claims.claim: Classical solvers are well-established and perform well for many linear, quadratic, and integer programming problems in finance.
key_claims.quote: However, for most instances correspondingtotheseclasses, thereareestablished, well- performing classical solvers, such as interior-point and simplex methods for linear and quadratic programs, or branch-and-bound and combinations with cutting-plane methods for integer programs.

key_claims.claim: These classical problems still form an excellent ground to benchmark and develop quantum optimization algorithms.
key_claims.quote: Nevertheless, these prob- lems form an excellent ground to benchmark and develop quantum optimization algorithms and potentially detect value in specific financial applications.

key_claims.claim: Most quantum portfolio optimization approaches use QUBO encodings with penalty terms, which only approximately enforce constraints and require substantial post-processing.
key_claims.quote: As discussed in Sec. VIIA2, so far, most quantum approaches to this use case employ QUBO for- mulations with binary or integer encodings, which result in anNPO-hard combinatorial problem and constraints that are converted into penalty terms [593] of the ob- jective function. Since these penalty terms only facili- tate approximate encoding of the constraints, additional substantial post-processing would be required to achieve reliable results.

key_claims.claim: It remains unclear how to systematically advance quantum approaches towards real-world complexity and value in optimal asset allocation.
key_claims.quote: However, we stress that it remains unclear how to sys- tematically advance towards the complexity and value frontier at which a real-world practical impact can be realized.
key_claims.location: Page 43, Section VII.A.3 Deep Dive: Optimal Asset Allocation

key_claims.claim: Development of quantum optimization solutions should move from simple Level 1 models to more complex Level 2 and 3 problems under uncertainty to be valuable for industry.
key_claims.quote: In particular, the development of new quan- tum optimization solutions should transition from cur- rent Level 1 investigations to Level 2 and 3 challenges, and with that drive research towards handling optimiza- tion problems under uncertainty in order to aim for valu- able contributions to the financial industry.
key_claims.location: Page 46, Section VII.A.3 Outlook within Deep Dive

key_claims.claim: Existing quantum optimization work in power grids focuses on small, illustrative problems with simple QUBO models that do not capture real-world complexity.
key_claims.quote: All of the works mentioned above have in common that they focus on small, illustrative problems and that they explore simple mathematical models (mostly QU- BOs) that do not capture the complexity of real-world use cases.

key_claims.claim: Although current quantum optimization work in power grids lacks direct practical impact, it may help advance theory, formulations, and understanding of practical requirements.
key_claims.quote: Although these works may not have a direct practical impact yet, they could help to pave the way for advancing the corresponding theory, problem formu- lations, algorithms, and to understand practical require- ments on optimization solutions to have practical impact.

key_claims.claim: MDPs for stochastic control quickly become difficult to solve and may be a good testbed for quantum approaches.
key_claims.quote: MDPs quickly become very difficult to solve due to the curse of dimensionality, cf. Sec. IVE. Thus, this might be an interesting domain for first small test cases to analyze the potential of corresponding quantum approaches.

key_claims.claim: Quantum optimization has vast potential but significant challenges remain in demonstrating practical quantum advantage.

open_questions.quote: There are several promising directions and open questions. What are lower bounds for various settings of quantum polynomial optimization? Beyond lower bounds, more in-depth focus on possible run time advantages of quantum algorithms is required.

open_questions.question: Can moment/SOS and SDP-based quantum algorithms provide speedups for broader classes of non-convex functions?

open_questions.question: What is the best possible quantum speedup for branch-and-bound on NP-hard problems?

open_questions.question: Which MIP reformulation approaches (Dantzig-Wolfe, Moment/SOS, completely positive) allow the best quantum speedups in continuous optimization?

open_questions.question: What advantage must a quantum subroutine provide to yield overall advantage for MIP algorithms, possibly including solution diversity?

problem_domains.problem: Evolution of quantum computing research and technologies
problem_domains.description: The paper addresses how quantum computing research is developing over time to support scientific advances and technological change.
problem_domains.quote: One of the fundamental questions hardly known is how quantum computing research is developing to support scientiﬁc advances and the evolution of path-breaking technologies for economic, industrial, and social change.

problem_domains.problem: Detection of main quantum computing technologies and trajectories
problem_domains.description: The study seeks to detect main QC technologies and technological trajectories that may become major sources of competitive advantage.
problem_domains.quote: This study can detect the main QC technologies, which may be major sources of competitive advantage for ﬁrms and nations to solve complex problems and satisfy new needs of people in society.

problem_domains.problem: Lack of scientometric studies on evolutionary networks of quantum computing
problem_domains.description: The paper notes a scarcity of scientometric analyses of QC evolutionary networks associated with new technologies.
problem_domains.quote: However, studies of scientometrics concerning evolutionary networks of QC associated with new technologies are scarce in the literature.

problem_domains.problem: Guiding R&D investments and innovation strategy in quantum technologies
problem_domains.description: The work addresses how to guide R&D and innovation strategy by understanding QC evolution and emerging technologies.
problem_domains.quote: The results of these studies can guide R&D investments and innovation strategy of ﬁrms and governments for supporting their competitive advantage in turbulent markets [33]–[37].

problem_domains.problem: Identifying emerging quantum technologies for innovative applications in markets
problem_domains.description: The study focuses on identifying emerging QC technologies that can be transferred into innovative market applications.
problem_domains.quote: This result suggests the potential transfer of QC research in new technologies for innovative applications, such as in quantum image processing for creating quantum images because this new technology has high technical performance in terms of computing speed, low storage requirements, and high security [56].

problem_domains.problem: Supporting strategic management of innovation for a quantum industry
problem_domains.description: The paper addresses how understanding QC evolution can support strategic innovation management and the emergence of a quantum industry.
problem_domains.quote: the results presented here clearly illustrate the main evolutionary paths of QC research that are increasingly based on growing connectivity between technologies and research ﬁelds, but a further detailed examination is needed for explaining the driving factors of the technological evolution and supporting an appropriate strategic management of innovation that supports a new quantum industry for the competitive advan- tage of ﬁrms and nations in turbulent markets.

solution_approaches.approach: Computational scientometrics for publication analyses
solution_approaches.description: The authors apply computational scientometric methods on publication data to explain the structure and evolution of quantum computing research and technologies.
solution_approaches.quote: This study confronts the question here by applying methods of computational scientometrics for publication analyses to explain the structure and evolution of quantum computing research and technologies over a 30-year period.

solution_approaches.approach: Maps of science / mapping of QC networks
solution_approaches.description: The study creates and analyzes maps of science based on keyword co-occurrence networks to show how QC fields and technologies evolve.
solution_approaches.quote: This study endeavors to create and analyze the mapping of QC over a 30-year time frame to detect different stages of the structure of network and the evolution of QC with main technological trajectories.

solution_approaches.approach: Keyword co-occurrence networks using DE tags
solution_approaches.description: The authors construct keyword co-occurrence networks from Web of Science author keywords (DEs) to identify QC research fields and technologies.
solution_approaches.quote: First, we used original keywords of articles (DEs) tag as the basis for detection of technologies related to QC. ... the units of analysis are the original keywords (DEs) of articles provided by authors to ﬁnd the QC research ﬁelds and technolo- gies and to create the interconnection network among nodes.
solution_approaches.location: Materials and Method, Section B, Page 2

solution_approaches.approach: Network centrality measures (degree, betweenness, closeness)
solution_approaches.description: The study uses degree, betweenness, and closeness centrality metrics to explore evolutionary behavior of nodes in the QC network.
solution_approaches.quote: Moreover, SCI2 Tool is applied to calculate metrics of these networks, such as degree centrality (DC), betweenness centrality (BC), and closeness centrality (CC) measures to explore the evolutionary behavior of different nodes within the network of QC over time.
solution_approaches.location: Materials and Method, Section C, Page 3

solution_approaches.approach: Time-sliced network analysis (1990–2000, 2001–2010, 2011–2020)
solution_approaches.description: The network is analyzed in three time periods to study changes in structure, connectivity, and emerging technologies.
solution_approaches.quote: The sample contains 14,132 articles split into three timespans, given by 1990–2000, 2001–2010, and 2011–2020.
solution_approaches.location: Materials and Method, Section A, Page 2

solution_approaches.approach: Identification of emerging technologies via network connectivity
solution_approaches.description: Emerging QC technologies are identified based on their appearance and connectivity patterns in the network over time.
solution_approaches.quote: The emerging technologies in QC from 2001 to 2010 are (see Table IV): quantum memory, adiabatic QC, topological QC, quantum walk, and quantum wire. Furthermore, over 2011- 2020, the emerging technologies are quantum image processing, quantum machine learning, and blind QC.

solution_approaches.approach: Morphological analysis of network shape
solution_approaches.description: The authors analyze the morphological evolution of the QC network from spheroid to irregular shapes to characterize stages of scientific and technological evolution.
solution_approaches.quote: Theoretical implications of this study show the morphological evolution of the network in quantum computing from a symmetric to an asymmetric shape driven by new inter-related research ﬁelds and emerging technolog- ical trajectories.

solution_approaches.approach: Innovation management guidance based on network metrics
solution_approaches.description: The study proposes using network measures (e.g., high degree centrality nodes) to guide R&D investment and innovation management decisions.
solution_approaches.quote: Findings here suggest best practices of innovation management based on R&D investments in new technological di- rections of quantum computing having a high potential for growth and impact in science and markets.

key_claims.claim: Quantum computing research is rapidly evolving with increasing network connectivity and complexity over 1990–2020.
key_claims.quote: Results reveal that the evolution of quantum computing from 1990 to 2020 has a considerable average increase of connectivity in the network (growth of degree centrality measure), a moderate increase of the average inﬂuence of nodes on the ﬂow between nodes (little growth of betweenness centrality measure), and a little reduction of the easiest access of each node to all other nodes (closeness centrality measure). This evolutionary dynamics is due to the increase in size and complexity of the network in quantum computing research over time.

key_claims.claim: The QC research network is transitioning from hardware-focused to software-focused research.
key_claims.quote: This study also suggests that the network of quantum computing has a transition from hardware to software research that supports accelerated evolution of technological pathways in quantum image processing, quantum machine learning, and quantum sensors.

key_claims.claim: Quantum image processing offers high computing speed, low storage requirements, and high security for innovative applications.
key_claims.quote: such as in quantum image processing for creating quantum images because this new technology has high technical performance in terms of computing speed, low storage requirements, and high security [56].

key_claims.claim: Quantum machine learning and blind quantum computing represent important emerging technological trajectories in QC.
key_claims.quote: Other emerging technologies in QC research are quantum machine learning based on the interaction of machine learning programs and quantum algorithms [57] and blind QC, such that quantum servers do not have full information about activities that users are computing for high security of tasks.

key_claims.claim: QC research co-evolves through high connectivity, moderate growth in node influence, and reduced average access due to network expansion.
key_claims.quote: First, QC research co-evolves with complex interactions driven by three evolutionary characteristics: a) a high con- nectivity between nodes of research ﬁelds and technologies; b) moderate growth of the average inﬂuence of nodes on the ﬂow between nodes within network; c) a reduction about the average easiest access of nodes to all other nodes because of a larger size and complexity of QC network over the course of time.

key_claims.claim: Certain QC research fields like quantum algorithms and quantum information act as master entities in the network.
key_claims.quote: Second, some research ﬁelds and technologies in QC network have a critical position, playing a role of master entity for connections of manifold research ﬁelds and technologies, such as quantum algorithm and information.

key_claims.claim: R&D investments directed at high-connectivity QC technologies can support competitive advantage in markets.
key_claims.quote: This study shows critical research ﬁelds and technologies in QC that are growing with a higher DC measure; R&D management can allocate economic resources towards these research ﬁelds and technologies (e.g., quantum memory, quantum image processing, quantum machine learning, etc.) to support scientiﬁc and technological development that create a background for competitive advantage in markets.

problem_domains.description: Portfolio optimization as a core financial task of allocating assets to maximize returns while minimizing risk, which becomes computationally intractable as the number of assets grows.
problem_domains.quote: Portfolio optimization is a critical task in finance that aims to allocate assets in a way that maximizes returns while minimizing risk. The seminal work of Harry Markowitz [1] on mean-variance optimization laid the foundation for modern portfolio theory. However, as the number of assets grows, the computational complexity of portfolio optimization increases exponentially, making it challenging to solve using classical optimization methods.

key_claims.claim: Quantum computing can improve financial portfolio optimization by addressing scalability and computational complexity issues.
key_claims.quote: Quantum computing has the potential to improve financial portfolio optimization by addressing scalability and computational complexity issues.

key_claims.claim: Quantum algorithms such as quantum annealing and QAOA can be adapted to solve the QUBO formulation of the portfolio optimization problem.
key_claims.quote: Quantum algorithms, such as quantum annealing and the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA), have shown promise in solving optimization problems. These algorithms can be adapted to tackle the Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) formulation of the portfolio optimization problem.

key_claims.claim: Quantum algorithms for QUBO-based portfolio optimization can theoretically provide a quadratic speedup over classical methods.
key_claims.quote: Quantum algorithms, such as quantum annealing and QAOA, have the potential to provide a quadratic speedup over classical methods [7]. The adiabatic algorithm for solving quadratic unconstrained binary o ptimization (QUBO) problems, which can be used to formulate portfolio optimization, has a time complexity of (𝑂(√𝑛)) [8].
key_claims.location: Section 5. Computational Complexity and Quantum Speedup, Page 6

key_claims.claim: The field of quantum computing is still in its early stages and faces several challenges before it can be widely adopted for financial applications.
key_claims.quote: However, the field of quantum computing is still in its early stages, and there are several challenges that nee d to be addressed before quantum computers can be widely adopted for financial applications.
key_claims.location: Page 2 (end of Introduction / start of Section 2)

key_claims.claim: Current quantum hardware is limited by noise, decoherence, and short coherence times, which restrict the complexity of portfolio optimization algorithms that can be implemented.
key_claims.quote: Quantum systems are inherently sensitive to environmental noise, which can lead to errors in the computation. The presence of noise can cause the quantum state to deviate fro m the desired state, resulting in inaccurate results. Decoherence, the loss of quantum coherence over time, limits the depth of quantum circuits that can be reliably executed [9]. Current quantum hardware has limited coherence times, which restricts the co mplexity of the algorithms that can be implemented.

key_claims.claim: The limited number of qubits in current quantum computers restricts the size of real-world portfolio optimization problems that can be solved.
key_claims.quote: The number of qubits available in current quantum computers is limited, which restricts the size of optimization problems that can be solved. To tackle real -world portfolio optimization problems with many assets, a sign ificant increase in the number of qubits is necessary.

key_claims.claim: Encoding large amounts of financial data into quantum states and extracting results creates an input/output bottleneck for quantum-classical hybrid portfolio optimization algorithms.
key_claims.quote: Efficiently encoding classical data into quantum states and extracting the results of quantum computa tions can be a bottleneck in quantum -classical hybrid algorithms [11]. Portfolio optimization involves processing large amounts of financial data, including asset prices, returns, and risk factors.

key_claims.claim: Many quantum optimization algorithms, including QAOA, currently have approximation ratios that are not yet competitive with state-of-the-art classical approximation algorithms.
key_claims.quote: Many quantum optimization algorithms, such as the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) [18], have approximation ratios that are not yet competitive with state -of-the-art classical approximation algorithms.

key_claims.claim: Integrating quantum computers into existing financial systems and workflows for portfolio optimization is challenging and requires robust quantum-classical hybrid architectures.
key_claims.quote: Integrating quantum computers into existing financial systems and workflows presents another challenge. Portfolio optimization is typically part of a larger investment management process that involves data sourcing, risk modeling, trade execution, and reporting. Seamlessly integrating quantum optimization routines into this process requires robust interfaces and compatibility with cl assical systems [19].
key_claims.location: Section 6.5. Integration with Classical Systems, Page 7

key_claims.claim: There is a talent gap in experts who understand both quantum algorithms and financial domain knowledge, which slows adoption of quantum portfolio optimization.
key_claims.quote: The field of quantum compu ting is still in its early stages, and there is a limited pool of talent with expertise in both quantum algorithms and financial domain knowledge. Developing and implementing quantum algorithms for portfolio optimization requires a multidisciplinary skill set, combining quantum information science, optimization theory, and financial mathematics [20].

key_claims.claim: Despite current challenges, the prospects of quantum computing in finance, particularly for portfolio optimization and other complex financial problems, are promising.
key_claims.quote: Despite these challenges, the prospects of quantum computing in finance are promisin g. As quantum hardware continues to improve and quantum algorithms become more refined, the application of quantum computing to portfolio optimization and other complex financial problems will likely become increasingly feasible.

key_claims.claim: Quantum algorithms can efficiently explore vast solution spaces and address the computational complexity of portfolio optimization with large asset pools and constraints.
key_claims.quote: These algorithms can efficiently explore vast solution spaces and tackle the computational complexity that arises in portfolio optimization problems with large asset pools and numerous constraints.

key_claims.claim: The practical applicability of quantum computing to portfolio optimization will improve as progress is made in hardware, error correction, and algorithm design.
key_claims.quote: As progress is made in quantum hardware, error correction, and algorithm design, the practical applicability of quantum computing to portfolio optimization and other financial problems will likely improve.
key_claims.location: Section 6. Challenges and Limitations (closing paragraph), Page 7

maturity_indicators.quote: Quantum computing presents a promising avenue for advancing portfolio optimization in finance. However, several challenges and limitations currently hinder its practical applicability:

open_questions.question: How can the effects of noise and decoherence be mitigated to improve the reliability of quantum computations for portfolio optimization?
open_questions.quote: Mitigating the effects of noise and decoherence is an active area of research, with techniques such as quantum error correction [13] and dynamical decoupling [14] being explored to improve the reliability  of quantum computations

open_questions.question: How can quantum hardware be scaled up in qubit count while maintaining high coherence times to handle real-world portfolio optimization problems with many assets?
open_questions.quote: To tackle real -world portfolio optimization problems with many assets, a sign ificant increase in the number of qubits is necessary. However, scaling up quantum hardware while maintaining high coherence times is an ongoing challenge [10].

open_questions.question: What efficient techniques can be developed for encoding large-scale financial data into quantum states and extracting results without excessive overhead?
open_questions.quote: Encoding this classical data into quantum states requires efficient techniques that minimize the overhead and preserve the required precision. Similarly, measuring and interpreting the results of quantum computations can be challenging, especially when dealing with high -dimensional quantum states. Developing effi cient input/output interfaces and data encoding schemes is an active area of research [17] to address this bottleneck.

open_questions.question: How can the approximation performance of quantum optimization algorithms like QAOA be improved to be competitive with state-of-the-art classical algorithms?
open_questions.quote: Rigorous analysis of the approximation performance of quantum optimization algorithms is an ongoing research area, aiming to improve the guarantees and understand the limitations of these algorithms.

open_questions.question: How can quantum optimization routines be seamlessly integrated into existing financial systems and workflows for portfolio optimization?
open_questions.quote: Seamlessly integrating quantum optimization routines into this process requires robust interfaces and compatibility with cl assical systems [19]. Developing quantum -classical hybrid architectures that leverage the strengths of both quantum and classical computing is an important step towards practical quantum finance applications.
open_questions.location: Section 6.5. Integration with Classical Systems, Page 7

open_questions.question: How can the talent gap in quantum algorithms and financial domain expertise be bridged to accelerate adoption of quantum technologies in finance?
open_questions.quote: Fostering collaboration between quantum experts and financial professionals, as well as investing in quantum education and training programs, is crucial for br idging the talent gap and accelerating the adoption of quantum technologies in finance.

open_questions.question: What theoretical foundations, efficient implementations, and quantum-inspired techniques are needed to fully realize the potential of quantum computing in finance?
open_questions.quote: Further investigations into the theoretical foundations of quantum algorithms, the development of efficient quantum implementations, and the exploration of novel quantum-inspired optimization techniques will be crucial in advancing the field.

open_questions.question: How can quantum computing be integrated into existing financial frameworks and quantum-ready financial models be developed to bridge the gap between theory and practice?
open_questions.quote: The integration of quantum computing into existing financial frameworks and the development of quantum -ready financial models will be necessary to bridge the gap between theory and practice .

problem_domains.description: Use of complex calculations to optimise large investment portfolios and manage financial risk, considering many variables such as asset correlations and market volatility.
problem_domains.quote: The finance and banking sector is another area where quantum computing has the potential to make a significant impact. Financial institutions rely on complex calculations for tasks such as risk assessment, portfolio optimisation and fraud detection.

problem_domains.description: Specific focus on optimising large investment portfolios and improving risk management by simulating market scenarios and processing large datasets.
problem_domains.quote: Quantum algorithms, such as the quantum approximate optimisation algorithm (QAOA), can excel at solving complex optimisation problems, which are common in finance. For example, they can optimise large investment portfolios by considering thousands of variables, including asset correlations, market volatility and risk factors.
problem_domains.location: Finance and banking – Risk analysis and portfolio optimisation

problem_domains.description: Improving risk assessment models and management of exposure to market fluctuations and economic downturns.
problem_domains.quote: Quantum algorithms could also improve risk management by simulating various market scenarios and identifying potential risks in real time. Quantum computers could enhance risk assessment models by processing large datasets and identifying correlations that classical computers may overlook.
problem_domains.location: Finance and banking – Risk analysis and portfolio optimisation

problem_domains.description: Detection of suspicious transactions and financial fraud in very large transaction datasets.
problem_domains.quote: Fraud detection is another area where quantum computing could have a significant impact. Financial institutions process vast amounts of data to identify suspicious transactions and detect fraud.

problem_domains.problem: Cryptography and blockchain security in finance
problem_domains.description: Threats to and redesign of cryptographic protocols and blockchain systems that secure financial transactions and data.
problem_domains.quote: The potential for quantum computers to break widely used cryptographic protocols represents a significant security risk, particularly for sensitive information in sectors such as finance, defence and healthcare.

problem_domains.problem: Cryptography and blockchain security in finance
problem_domains.description: Vulnerability of blockchain technologies and need for quantum-safe blockchain protocols.
problem_domains.quote: Blockchain technologies, which rely on cryptographic security, may also be affected by quantum computing. Quantum computers could potentially break the cryptographic hashes that secure blockchain transactions, necessitating the development of quantum-safe blockchain protocols.
problem_domains.location: Finance and banking – Cryptography and blockchain

problem_domains.description: Need for financial institutions to update cryptographic systems to protect against quantum attacks and secure sensitive financial transactions.
problem_domains.quote: Financial institutions will need to update their cryptographic systems to protect against quantum attacks, and quantum cryptography could provide a new level of security for sensitive financial transactions.
problem_domains.location: Defence and national security – Quantum-safe security

problem_domains.quote: For example, quantum algorithms could optimise the logistics of shipping goods, minimising fuel consumption and carbon emissions.

problem_domains.quote: By analysing vast amounts of climate data, quantum computing could help develop more effective strategies for mitigating global warming, such as optimising carbon capture technologies or identifying regions most vulnerable to climate impacts.

problem_domains.description: The paper presents the need to accelerate discovery of new materials for environmentally friendly products like biodegradable plastics and energy-efficient batteries.
problem_domains.quote: Quantum simulations of molecular interactions could accelerate the discovery of new materials for use in environmentally friendly products, such as biodegradable plastics, energy-efficient batteries and low-emission construction materials.

problem_domains.description: The paper mentions the challenge of optimising energy grids as a complex problem that quantum computers could address.

key_claims.claim: Quantum computing could play a critical role in addressing global challenges such as climate change, energy efficiency and sustainable development.

key_claims.claim: Quantum computing can tackle complex financial problems that are practically impossible for classical computers to solve efficiently.
key_claims.quote: This superposition characteristic enables quantum computers to perform calculations at an unprecedented speed and tackle complex problems that are practically impossible for classical computers to solve efﬁciently .

key_claims.claim: Quantum computing promises breakthroughs in key financial tasks such as credit scoring, fraud detection, option pricing, investment recommendation, and dynamic portfolio optimization.
The proposed variant of the CRA quantum algorithm offers a more realistic software solution for credit risk analysis and holds promise for the financial sector as quantum technology advances.
key_claims.quote: This article proposed a variant of the CRA quantum algorithm addressing the limitations of other implementations by enhancing risk models to consider multiple systemic risk factors, allowing ﬂexibility in input data, and testing through classical simulation and the use of quantum processing units (QPU). While it increases circuit complexity , this variant offers a more realistic software solution and holds promise for the ﬁnancial sector as quantum technology advances.
key_claims.location: Page 4, paragraph on March 2023 peer-reviewed paper

key_claims.claim: Quantum computing may provide advantages in speed or precision even for problems that are not classically intractable.
key_claims.quote: In the ﬁnancial domain, there are many possible applications of quantum that could have a potential advantage over classical counterparts. QC allows the use of another type of math that can be exploited to solve problems that may not be classically intractable but in which there can still be some advantage to be gained. This advantage can be deﬁned either in the speed domain, reaching the same outcome faster , or in the precision domain, reaching a ﬁner solution granularity that was not previously possible.
key_claims.location: Page 5, Section V. Challenges and Future Perspectives

key_claims.claim: Classical solutions for fraud detection and credit scoring have issues such as unbalanced datasets and difficulty in choosing meaningful input features, motivating exploration of quantum approaches.

key_claims.claim: Quantum computing is revolutionizing finance by tackling complex computations in risk management, portfolio allocation, and cryptography.
key_claims.quote: QC is revolutionizing finance this outlines its capability in tackling complicate computations in risk management, portfolio allocation and cryptography.

key_claims.claim: Quantum algorithms such as Shor’s, Grover’s, QAOA, and VQE have significant implications for optimization, cryptography, and simulation problems in finance.
key_claims.quote: Considering the above mentioned properties, QC has significant implications in optimization, cryptography, and simulation problems in the finance area. As a matter of fact, several quantum algorithms have a direct bearing and application in finance:
key_claims.location: II. FUNDAMENTALS OF QUANTUM COMPUTING IN FINANCE, Page 2

key_claims.claim: Quantum Monte Carlo algorithms can attain quadratic speedup over classical Monte Carlo, drastically improving accuracy and efficiency of risk evaluation.
key_claims.quote: Quantum Computing evolves over this historic method by employing quantum Monte Carlo algorithms, which can attain quadratic speedup compared to classical techniques [16]. This can drastically improve accuracy and efficiency of risk evaluation in financial markets.
key_claims.location: III. CURRENT TRENDS IN QUANTUM FINANCE – A. Quantum Applications in Financial Modeling, Page 3

key_claims.claim: Shor’s algorithm poses a major problem to conventional cryptosystems like RSA and ECC, creating a significant cryptographic threat for finance.
key_claims.quote: Namely Shor’s algorithm is the most effective to break widely used today public-key cryptographic protocol such as RSA and ECC in view of factoring large prime numbers [17].
key_claims.location: III. CURRENT TRENDS IN QUANTUM FINANCE – B. Quantum Cryptography & Blockchain in Finance, Page 3

key_claims.claim: Quantum-resistant blockchains and post-quantum cryptography are critical steps toward securing decentralized financial systems against quantum attacks.
key_claims.quote: However, the development of quantum resistant blockchains, incorporating quantum-safe encryption techniques, is a critical tread toward securing decentralized financial systems [19].
key_claims.location: III. CURRENT TRENDS IN QUANTUM FINANCE – B. Quantum Cryptography & Blockchain in Finance, Page 3

key_claims.claim: Quantum machine learning can handle high-dimensional and noisy financial data more effectively than classical models, enhancing trading strategies and anomaly detection.
key_claims.quote: As opposed to classical models, that struggle with high-dimensional and noisy financial data, quantum algorithms can perform variable selection and optimization more effectively. This can enhance trading strategies, high-frequency trading, and market anomaly detection.
key_claims.location: III. CURRENT TRENDS IN QUANTUM FINANCE – C. Quantum Machine Learning in Trading & Forecasting, Page 4

key_claims.claim: Current quantum devices are NISQ and do not yet allow full exploitation of exponential qubit growth, limiting practical financial applications.
key_claims.quote: Quantum computing is yet to be practically applied in the financial industry due to the limited advancement of quantum hardware today. However, the recent technological developments from companies like IBM, Google, and D-Wave do not yet belong to the next generation quantum computers where in principle the exponential growth of the number of qubits can be fully exploited, as the current state of the art quantum devices are still noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices where the errors of the qubits are significantly high, and their coherence time is limited insufficiently short .
key_claims.location: IV. CHALLENGES & LIMITATIONS – A. Hardware Limitations, Page 4

key_claims.claim: Few current quantum processors have enough qubits to solve real-life financial problems such as quantum portfolio optimization.
key_claims.quote: Scalability: Few current quantum processors possess enough number of qubits to solve the real life problems in the fields of finance. For instance, quantum portfolio optimization can be done with a few hundred or thousand logical qubits, while the present generation quantum processors contain up to tens to low hundred noisy qubits [24].
key_claims.location: IV. CHALLENGES & LIMITATIONS – A. Hardware Limitations, Page 4

key_claims.claim: Many financial problems do not yet have proven quantum advantage, and the benefits of algorithms like QAOA and VQE for large-scale applications are still debated.
key_claims.quote:
While quantum algorithms promise significant speedup over classical algorithms, many financial problems do not yet have proven quantum advantage. Several theoretical and computational challenges remain:
x Lack of Quantum Speedup for Many Problems: Not all financial problems benefit from quantum acceleration. For example, some optimization and machine learning tasks can be efficiently solved using classical heuristics and high-performance computing (HPC) systems. Moreover, the advantage provided by quantum algorithms like QAOA and VQE is still being debated for large-scale practical applications [25].
key_claims.location: IV. CHALLENGES & LIMITATIONS – Algorithmic and Theoretical Challenges, Page 4

key_claims.claim: Hybrid quantum-classical models introduce computational overhead due to frequent switching between resources, limiting efficiency.
key_claims.quote: Most quantum computing applications in finance currently rely on hybrid quantum-classical approaches, where quantum subroutines are integrated with classical algorithms. These hybrid models introduce additional computational overhead due to frequent switching between classical and quantum resources, limiting their overall efficiency [26].
key_claims.location: IV. CHALLENGES & LIMITATIONS – Algorithmic and Theoretical Challenges, Page 4

key_claims.claim: Integration with existing financial systems requires significant investment in software, expertise, and hardware, posing an adoption barrier.
key_claims.quote: Traditional financial institutions operate on well-established classical computing infrastructures. Transitioning to quantum-based systems requires significant investment in new software architectures, quantum programming expertise, and hardware infrastructure.
key_claims.location: IV. CHALLENGES & LIMITATIONS – B. Financial Industry Adoption Barriers, Page 4

key_claims.claim: Quantum advantage in finance is expected to emerge gradually, with short-term focus on hybrid algorithms and testing quantum annealers, mid-term fault-tolerant applications, and long-term fully scalable systems.
key_claims.quote:
x Short-Term (0–5 years) : The emphasis will be made on the development of hybrid quantum- classical algorithms, as well as the advanced quantum error correction. In this context, financial companies will keep on testing quantum annealers (i.e., D-Wave) in operational applications such as portfolio management and risk analysis.
x Mid-Term (5–10 years):  Increased qubit counts and reduced error rates will make fault-tolerant quantum computing feasible for select financial applications, such as high-frequency trading and derivatives pricing.
x Long-Term (10+ years):  Fully scalable quantum computers could revolutionize financial systems, enabling real-time Monte Carlo simulations, complex derivatives modeling, and unbreakable quantum cryptography.
key_claims.location: V. FUTURE PROSPECTS & EMERGING RESEARCH DIRECTIONS – A. Quantum Advantage in Finance: Expected Timeline, Page 5

key_claims.claim: Quantum computing may bring significant benefits in finance such as faster portfolio optimization, improved risk control, enhanced cryptographic safety, and effective financial modelling.
key_claims.quote: While QC has the capabilities to disrupt almost every sector of the economy, in the scholarly field of finance, it may bring several significant benefits such as a higher rate of creation for portfolio optimization, improved risk control, enhanced levels of cryptographic safety, and effective financial modelling.
key_claims.location: VI. CONCLUSION – A. Summary of Key Findings, Page 5-6

key_claims.claim: Quantum supremacy in finance within the next five to ten years is considered a sound inference by the authors.
key_claims.quote: Stepping away from unfounded speculations, surmising that quantum supremacy will be real in the next five to ten years is a sound inference for a couple of reasons.

problem_domains.description: The paper frames many real-world problems as too complex and variable for classical computers to handle satisfactorily.
problem_domains.quote: Real world problems are extremely complex and keep varying thereby handling them on a classical computer produces unsatisfactory in many cases.

problem_domains.problem: Simulation of atoms and molecules / multi-dimensional computational spaces
problem_domains.description: Classical processors are described as failing on problems like simulating atoms and molecules and solving multi-dimensional computational spaces.
problem_domains.quote: Even these powerful processors come with a few limitations and fail to solve problems like simulation of atoms and molecules, solve multi-dimensional computational spaces.

problem_domains.description: Integer factorization of large numbers is presented as a hard computational problem for classical computers.
problem_domains.quote: In 1994, Peter Shor devised an algorithm (Shor’s algorithm) to solve a popular number theory problem of integer factorization (Shor, 1994). The Shor’s algorithm allowed for factorization in polynomial time complexity while the best algorithm at that time consumed exponential time complexity.

problem_domains.problem: Fast database search in unstructured datasets
problem_domains.description: Searching an unstructured database is framed as requiring O(N) time classically.
problem_domains.quote: In classical computing, finding a specific item in an N-item database required sequential checks, taking O(N) time.
problem_domains.location: 3.2 Lov Grover Fast Database Search, Page 9

problem_domains.problem: Determining whether a function is constant or balanced
problem_domains.description: The Deutsch-Jozsa problem is described as requiring exponential evaluations classically.
problem_domains.quote: For classical computers, solving this problem requires O(2n) evaluations of the function, since each input must be checked to determine the function’s behavior.

problem_domains.problem: Healthcare molecular simulations and complex medical computations
problem_domains.description: Healthcare tasks like molecular simulations and complex operations are described as requiring very large processing and being time-limited.
problem_domains.quote: In healthcare, things are often connected in complicated ways, where there are relations and structures between molecules and electrons. The processing requirement for performing operations and tasks in the domain of medicine is very big concerning the problem. Time is one of the largest limiting factors.

problem_domains.description: Radiotherapy planning is framed as a complicated optimization problem needing many simulations to minimize damage to healthy tissue.
problem_domains.quote: Radiology is a very complicated method; therefore, it requires highly specific and advanced computers to perform operations accurately. This involves executing various operations to achieve the optimal outcome.

problem_domains.description: Discovering new drugs is described as difficult due to complex interactions and modern factors like climate change and pollution.
problem_domains.quote: In the modern period, it is difficult to develop new forms of medicine and drugs due to various factors like climate change, pollution, food contamination, and allergies.

problem_domains.problem: Pricing of diagnosis / healthcare risk analysis and fraud in medical insurance
problem_domains.description: Developing pricing schemes and performing risk analysis in healthcare, including fraud detection in medical insurance, is presented as a challenge.
problem_domains.quote: One of the main challenges is to develop a pricing scheme in the domain of healthcare and medicine, which will cause hurdles in the medicine industry.

problem_domains.problem: Fraud detection in banking and financial transactions
problem_domains.description: Fraud detection is described as critical but limited by rules-based and statistical methods that miss sophisticated schemes and often act after the fact.
problem_domains.quote: Fraud detection is a critical function for banks to maintain trust with their customers and to protect their assets. However, traditional methods rely on rules-based systems and statistical analysis thus limiting their ability to detect sophisticated fraud schemes.

problem_domains.description: Existing machine-learning-based fraud systems are said to detect fraud only after it has occurred, not in real time.
problem_domains.quote: The utilization of machine learning has seen a growing application in the identification of fraudulent transactions but majority of the existing systems are only capable of detecting deceitful activities after they have taken place, rather than in real-time.

problem_domains.problem: Financial risk management and Value at Risk / CVaR estimation

problem_domains.problem: Portfolio optimization and complex risk analysis

maturity_indicators.quote: All these proposals were tested on quantum computers developed in the Bell labs and IBM.
The invention of three qubit quantum machine in 1999 and seven qubit quantum machines in 2000 further optimized these techniques

For instance, Google’s Willow chip recently showcas ed pioneering results in quantum error correction, demonstrating performance below the critical threshold where increasing physical qubits lead to an exponential reduction in logical error rates
IBM’s roadmap anticipates the unveiling of processors such as “Flamingo” (1,386  qubits) and “Kookaburra” (4,158 qubits) by 2025
Microsoft’s topological qubits, exemplified by their “Majorana 1” chip introduced in early 2025, represent a distinct approach.
Organizations like PayPal and HSBC are collaborating with quantum firms to enhance fraud detection and cybersecurity.

Companies like JPMorgan Chase and Goldman Sachs are exploring quantum algorithms (e.g., QAOA (Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm), Quantum Monte Carlo) for portfolio optimization and complex risk analysis
Recent advancements include China’s intercontinental QKD via the Micius satellite and the development of metropolitan fibre -optic quantum networks.
Quantum simulations continue to be a major area of research due to their wide-ranging possibilities.
However, the physical realization of a quantum computer remains a major challenge.
Current quantum processors, such as those developed by IBM, Google, and other research institutions, have demonstrated computational capabilities beyond cl assical systems for specific problems.
However, these systems are still in their infancy, suffering from issues like qubit decoherence, error rates, and limited connectivity.

The central obstacle to realizing useful quantum computation is the achievement of fault-tolerant quantum systems through sound quantum error correction (QEC) (Lidar & Brun, 2013; Devitt et al., 2013 ; Roffe, 2019).
maturity_indicators.location: Section 6.8 The Central Challenge of Quantum Error Correction, Page 18

key_claims.quote: Qubits are highly sensitive to environmental noise, leading to decoherence [7]. Error correction is essential but resource-intensive, often requiring thousands of physical qubits to encode a single logical qubit [9].

key_claims.claim: Algorithmic progress in quantum computing lags behind hardware, and most landmark algorithms require fault-tolerant devices.
key_claims.quote: Algorithmic progress lags behind hardware. Classical redundancy does not apply to quantum systems due to the no-cloning theorem. While landmark algorithms exist, most require fault-tolerant devices [13].

key_claims.claim: The near future of quantum computing lies in NISQ devices, with early applications expected in chemistry and optimization.
key_claims.quote: The near future lies in NISQ devices, which may yield early applications in chemistry and optimization [15].

key_claims.claim: No single hardware platform has yet achieved the optimal balance of scale and fidelity needed for universal fault-tolerant quantum computation.
key_claims.quote: the heterogeneous hardware landscape (Superconducting vs. Trapped Ion systems) illustrates that no single platform has yet achieved the optimal balance of scale and fidelity for universal fault-tolerant computation.

maturity_indicators.quote: VQE and similar algorithms may predict binding affinities and reaction pathways, reducing the time and cost of drug development [4].

Google’s 2019 demonstration with the 53-qubit Sycamore processor claimed such a milestone by executing random circuit sampling in 200 seconds, a task estimated to require 10,000 years on a classical machine [2].
Finance depends on complex optimization and risk modeling. Quantum algorithms such as QAOA and quantum Monte Carlo may enhance portfolio optimization, derivative pricing, and risk simulations.
The long-term vision is a fault-tolerant universal quantum computer. Achieving it demands interdisciplinary collaboration across physics, engineering, and computer science.

open_questions.question: How can the fidelity necessary for large-scale quantum error correction be achieved to enable fault-tolerant quantum computing?
open_questions.quote: Quantum error correction codes, such as surface codes, can detect and correct errors through indirect measurements, but achieving the fidelity necessary for large-scale error correction remains an engineering challenge [8].

open_questions.question: How can quantum processors be scaled to millions of qubits given current wiring, cryogenics, gate speed, and architectural challenges?
open_questions.quote: Scaling quantum processors requires integrating millions of qubits. Superconducting qubits face wiring and cryogenics challenges, while trapped ions encounter slower gate speeds and complexity at large ion counts [11][12].

open_questions.question: How can NISQ-era algorithms like VQE and QAOA be improved to overcome issues such as barren plateaus and be made practically useful?
open_questions.quote: NISQ-era algorithms such as VQE and QAOA combine classical optimization with quantum state preparation, but challenges like barren plateaus remain [14].

open_questions.question: What global collaborative efforts among academia, industry, and governments are needed to overcome the scientific and engineering barriers to large-scale quantum computing?
open_questions.quote: Global collaboration among academia, industry, and governments will be vital for overcoming scientific and engineering barriers.

key_claims.claim: Quantum computing can revolutionize risk management, portfolio optimization, market forecasting, and data protection in finance.
key_claims.quote: This chapter introduces the revolutionary potential of quantum computing in finance, referencing its promise to revolutionize risk management, portfolio optimization, market forecasting, and data protection.

key_claims.claim: Classical financial models like Monte Carlo, Black-Scholes, and Markowitz portfolio theory are computationally burdensome and limited in volatile, interconnected markets.
key_claims.quote: These classical approaches are computationally burdensome when addressing interconnected, real- time challenges in volatile mar- kets.

key_claims.claim: Quantum algorithms can dramatically decrease computational complexity and improve decision-making efficiency in finance.
key_claims.quote: while illustrating how the advances dramatically decrease com- putational complexity and improve decision- making efficiency.

key_claims.claim: Quantum models provide exponential computational power and can better capture the dynamic, interdependent nature of financial ecosystems than classical models.
key_claims.quote: Quantum models provide a compelling alternative in terms of exponential compu- tational power and the ability to examine multiple variables and scenarios simultane- ously.
